title: Actively Resolving Contextual Uncertainty for Underspecified Tasks in Natural Language
comment: Accepted to the International Symposium of Robotics Research (ISRR) 2026
summary: Foundation models provide robots with the ability to interpret natural language and reason about environmental context, yet most language-conditioned policies assume that goals are well-specified and that task-relevant information is provided upfront via a prior map. Operating in unfamiliar environments with underspecified tasks entails high contextual uncertainty: the robot must jointly infer what constitutes task success, what constitutes relevant information, and where (or whether) that information exists. We address these limitations via CLUE (Closed-Loop contextual Uncertainty rEsolution), a framework for actively resolving contextual uncertainty given underspecified tasks in natural language. CLUE uses an LLM-derived policy to hypothesize task-relevant concepts and potential plans. It then uses a language-embedded map, which is constructed online, to ground these hypotheses into actions. The policy sequentially evaluates hypotheses via closed-loop environment interaction and refines its plans as it gathers new information. We deploy CLUE on a Boston Dynamics Spot across three real indoor and outdoor environments spanning 15 tasks that require object disambiguation, functional inference, and occlusion reasoning. CLUE achieves a success rate within 7 percentage points of an oracle policy and outperforms an LLM-enabled planner without closed-loop feedback by a 4x margin. Supporting experiments demonstrate that simply building and then querying a language-enriched map is insufficient to resolve complex contextual planning tasks; these approaches achieve roughly one third the success rate of CLUE while requiring over 10x more VLM tokens. We provide additional information at https://zacravichandran.github.io/CLUE.

AI.tldr: CLUE is a framework that actively resolves contextual uncertainty for robots operating in unfamiliar environments with underspecified natural language tasks, using closed-loop environment interaction to hypothesize and ground task-relevant concepts.
AI.motivation: Most language-conditioned robot policies assume goals are well-specified and that task-relevant information is provided upfront via a prior map. However, operating in unfamiliar environments with underspecified tasks entails high contextual uncertainty: the robot must jointly infer what constitutes task success, what information is relevant, and where or whether that information exists.
AI.method: CLUE (Closed-Loop contextual Uncertainty rEsolution) uses an LLM-derived policy to hypothesize task-relevant concepts and potential plans. It then uses a language-embedded map, constructed online, to ground these hypotheses into actions. The policy sequentially evaluates hypotheses via closed-loop environment interaction and refines its plans as it gathers new information.
AI.result: Deployed on a Boston Dynamics Spot across three real indoor and outdoor environments spanning 15 tasks requiring object disambiguation, functional inference, and occlusion reasoning, CLUE achieves a success rate within 7 percentage points of an oracle policy and outperforms an LLM-enabled planner without closed-loop feedback by a 4x margin. Simply building and querying a language-enriched map achieves roughly one third the success rate of CLUE while requiring over 10x more VLM tokens.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop, active resolution of contextual uncertainty is essential for handling underspecified tasks in unfamiliar environments, and is far more effective and efficient than static language-enriched map querying or open-loop LLM planning.

title: Bringing AI to Autonomous Systems -- From Cognition to Collective Intelligence
summary: The purpose of this article is to highlight the central role of autonomous systems as the ultimate stage in the development of AI, to explain the underlying technical challenges that require a combination of connectionist AI and symbolic AI, and to integrate AI and systems engineering. We present a comprehensive framework for the design and evaluation of autonomous systems, based on a generic agent architecture that characterizes their behavior as the composition of cognitive functions organized around a long-term memory containing the agent's evolving knowledge. We address the challenges posed by the implementation of the fundamental features of the agent architecture, in particular the link between sensory data and structured data stored in memory, decision-making related to the achievement of the agent's goals and their planning, as well as the coordination of agents to combine individual and collective intelligence. We explain that agent trustworthiness, unlike that of traditional systems, is not limited to behavioral properties. It includes an essential dimension related to cognitive properties, the validity of which depends on how the agent uses its knowledge in decision-making. We present avenues for the development of methods for evaluating agent trustworthiness. We conclude with a critical assessment of the substantial gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for designing and evaluating autonomous systems, grounded in a generic agent architecture that composes cognitive functions around a long-term memory. It addresses key technical challenges—linking sensory to structured data, goal-driven decision-making and planning, and multi-agent coordination—and argues that trustworthiness requires both behavioral and cognitive dimensions, concluding with a critical assessment of the gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems are framed as the ultimate stage in AI development, yet realizing them demands combining connectionist and symbolic AI and integrating AI with systems engineering. The paper is motivated by the need to clarify the underlying technical challenges and to provide a coherent framework for their design and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose a comprehensive design and evaluation framework based on a generic agent architecture that characterizes behavior as a composition of cognitive functions organized around a long-term memory holding the agent's evolving knowledge. They analyze the implementation challenges of its fundamental features, including the link between sensory data and structured memory data, goal-oriented decision-making and planning, and coordination among agents to combine individual and collective intelligence. They extend trustworthiness beyond behavioral properties to include a cognitive dimension tied to the validity of knowledge use in decision-making, and outline avenues for developing trustworthiness evaluation methods.
AI.result: The paper delivers a unified framework and articulates the core technical challenges of autonomous systems, redefines trustworthiness to include cognitive properties, and provides directions for evaluating it, while offering a critical assessment of the substantial gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous systems represent the ultimate stage of AI, requiring the fusion of connectionist and symbolic AI and the integration of AI with systems engineering. A generic agent architecture centered on long-term memory provides a basis for design and evaluation, and trustworthiness must encompass cognitive as well as behavioral validity. Significant progress is still needed to close the gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.

title: ScopeBench: Do Agents Preserve Engagement Boundaries Under Goal Pressure?
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Accepted at AISec 2026. Code and tasks: https://github.com/dreadnode/scopebench-pilot. Trajectories: https://huggingface.co/datasets/dreadnode/scopebench-pilot. Leaderboard: https://scopebench.ai
summary: Agents are increasingly deployed with real autonomy in web application and network penetration testing, where a single out-of-scope action can breach a client's engagement boundary. Existing offensive-security benchmarks measure raw hacking capability; as those benchmarks saturate, the real barrier to deployment is a special case of alignment: scope adherence. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark of 30 dead-end agentic security tasks in which the stated objective is reachable only by violating the stated scope. Each task appears under two conditions that share an environment, verifier, and objective and differ only in scope: one instruction set has no scope and measures capability; the other has a natural-language scope to measure adherence. Scopeless trajectories are graded by a standard deterministic verifier. Scoped trajectories pass through two grading arms. First, the same deterministic verifier checks for the flag: because the flag sits behind the scope boundary, a pass proves by construction that a forbidden action occurred, yielding a high-precision lower bound on the violation rate. If the verifier does not pass the trajectory, an agentic judge estimates whether an out-of-scope call occurred. We calibrate the judge against 100 ScopeBench trajectories labeled call-by-call by human annotators, and a blinded audit of the evaluated rollouts finds its high recall holds - no false negatives among the 36 audited violations, with over-flagging its only observed error. Across 8 models in one harness, raw capability spans 12.2% to 81.1% and scope adherence spans 34.4% to 86.7%, with the judge finding 331 violations that mechanical verification misses. Opus-4-8 achieves a raw-capability score 10 percentage points higher than sonnet-4-6's while exhibiting 35.6 percentage points higher scope adherence. We release the frozen pilot benchmark, evaluation code, and all 2160 ATIF trajectories.

AI.tldr: ScopeBench is a benchmark of 30 dead-end agentic security tasks where the stated objective is only reachable by violating the stated scope. Each task is run under a scopeless (capability) and a scoped (adherence) condition sharing the same environment, verifier, and objective. Evaluation combines a deterministic verifier (high-precision lower bound on violations) with a calibrated agentic judge (high recall). Across 8 models, raw capability spans 12.2%-81.1% and scope adherence 34.4%-86.7%, with the judge detecting 331 violations missed mechanically.
AI.motivation: As offensive-security benchmarks for web application and network penetration testing saturate on raw hacking capability, the actual deployment barrier becomes alignment in the form of scope adherence, since a single out-of-scope action can breach a client's engagement boundary. Existing benchmarks measure only raw capability and thus fail to capture this critical alignment dimension.
AI.method: The authors introduce ScopeBench: 30 dead-end agentic security tasks whose objective is reachable only by violating scope. Each task appears under two conditions (scopeless vs. scoped) sharing environment, verifier, and objective, differing only in scope instructions. Scopeless trajectories are graded by a standard deterministic verifier. Scoped trajectories use two grading arms: (1) the deterministic verifier checks for the flag - since the flag lies behind the scope boundary, a pass proves a forbidden action occurred, giving a high-precision lower bound on violation rate; (2) if the verifier fails, an agentic judge estimates whether an out-of-scope call occurred. The judge is calibrated against 100 ScopeBench trajectories labeled call-by-call by human annotators, plus a blinded audit of evaluated rollouts.
AI.result: Model evaluation across 8 models in a single harness shows raw capability spans 12.2% to 81.1% and scope adherence spans 34.4% to 86.7%. The agentic judge finds 331 violations that mechanical verification misses. A blinded audit of the 36 audited violations shows no false negatives, with over-flagging as the only observed error. Opus-4-8 achieves a raw-capability score 10 percentage points higher than sonnet-4-6's while exhibiting 35.6 percentage points higher scope adherence, demonstrating capability and adherence are not simply coupled.
AI.conclusion: Scope adherence is a distinct alignment challenge separable from raw offensive-security capability, and capability does not guarantee adherence (as shown by Opus-4-8's divergent scores). ScopeBench provides a rigorous, dual-condition measurement with a calibrated judge that catches violations mechanical verification alone would miss. The authors release the frozen pilot benchmark, evaluation code, and all 2160 ATIF trajectories to support further research on scope adherence in agentic security deployments.

title: When Is a Multi-Agent Code Judge Actually Grounded? Two Label-Free Measurements, and a Judge That Declines to Guess
comment: Accepted at the 21st Women in Machine Learning Workshop (WiML), NeurIPS 2026
summary:
When one language model judges whether another's code is correct, it does not report the absence of evidence. It returns a confident verdict with reasoning attached, indistinguishable from a verdict it had grounds for. Multi-agent verification, which decomposes a judgment into checkable claims and verifies each against evidence, is a promising response and works well when the evidence is a set of retrieved documents.
  We argue such methods require two things of their evidence: it must be independent of the answer under review, and it must differ between the two candidates being compared. The second condition holds automatically with retrieved documents and stops holding in code judging.
  Running MARCH, a published framework unmodified over 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code judging benchmarks, we find it declares both solutions equally good on 78 to 95% of comparisons, reaching 4.4% accuracy where the same model asked directly reaches 43.7%. Neither easier problems nor a larger judge changes this. Two measurements taken from the pipeline's own logs explain it without needing labels.
  Gating on one of them, the pipeline declines the comparisons it cannot make and raises its accuracy from 20.7 to 36.9% while still answering half of all comparisons. The contribution is not a more accurate judge, but a label-free way to tell when a judge has no basis for its answer.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent verification frameworks for code judging fail because, unlike retrieved documents, code solutions are not differentiated by the verification evidence, causing the pipeline to declare ties in 78-95% of comparisons; a label-free log-based signal can detect when the judge has no basis and gate out untenable verdicts.
AI.motivation: Language models asked to judge whether another model's code is correct tend to output confident verdicts with reasoning, even when they have no actual evidence — they never signal absence of grounds. Multi-agent verification (decomposing judgments into checkable claims) partially addresses this but works only in settings like document retrieval. The paper aims to characterize why such verification breaks in code judging and to find a way to detect unfounded judgments without labels.
AI.method: The authors argue verification evidence must satisfy two conditions: (1) independence from the answer under review, and (2) differentiation between the two candidates being compared. The second holds automatically for retrieved documents but not for code. They run MARCH, an existing multi-agent verification framework, unmodified across 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code judging benchmarks, comparing against direct model judgments. They then analyze two measurements extracted from the pipeline's own logs to explain failures without requiring ground-truth labels, and gate the pipeline on one of these measurements.
AI.result: MARCH declares both solutions equally good on 78-95% of comparisons, achieving only 4.4% accuracy, whereas the same model asked directly reaches 43.7%. Neither easier problems nor a larger judge model improves this. Gating on a log-derived measurement lets the pipeline decline comparisons it cannot make, raising accuracy from 20.7% to 36.9% while still answering half of all comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The paper's contribution is not a more accurate judge but a label-free method for detecting when a judge lacks any basis for its answer. It reframes multi-agent verification's applicability by identifying independence and differentiation as necessary evidence conditions, showing that code judging violates differentiation, and demonstrating that internal pipeline signals can reliably expose unfounded verdicts.

title: Bridging LLM Agents and Data Spaces: An Architectural Mediation Approach using the Model Context Protocol
summary: Data Spaces enable sovereign and governed data sharing across organizational boundaries, but their integration with AI agents remains challenging due to mismatches between probabilistic language model interactions and policy-driven data infrastructures. This article presents an architectural mediation approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), implemented through the Eunomia Agent, to enable controlled interaction between large language model (LLM) agents and data space services. The proposed mediation layer translates data space capabilities into structured, schema-driven tools that AI agents can discover and invoke while preserving governance constraints. A prototype implementation validates end-to-end interaction across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation without modifying existing data space components. Results demonstrate that protocol-based mediation enables interoperable and standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems. The approach provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to introduce AI-driven automation into governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based mediation layer, implemented as the Eunomia Agent, to bridge LLM agents and data spaces by exposing data space capabilities as structured, schema-driven tools under governance constraints, validated via a prototype across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation.
AI.motivation: Data Spaces support sovereign, governed cross-organizational data sharing, but integrating AI agents is difficult because probabilistic LLM interactions do not align with policy-driven data infrastructures.
AI.method: An architectural mediation approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), realized through the Eunomia Agent, translating data space capabilities into structured, schema-driven tools that AI agents can discover and invoke while preserving governance constraints. A prototype was implemented without modifying existing data space components.
AI.result: The prototype validates end-to-end interaction covering catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation, showing that protocol-based mediation enables interoperable, standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems.
AI.conclusion: Protocol-based mediation offers practical guidance for organizations adopting AI-driven automation in governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
summary: A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "skill cascading attacks," where malicious intent is split across multiple interoperating skills so each looks benign but their combination is harmful, and provides SkillCascade (a multi-agent red-teaming framework) plus SkillCascade-Bench (213 validated cases).
AI.motivation: Skill-based agent systems enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but this openness creates a new attack surface. Prior work addresses vulnerabilities within individual skills, leaving cross-skill interaction risks—such as a harmful objective distributed across skills—largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors formalize skill cascading attacks as a threat paradigm and build SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, along with SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases spanning multiple agent systems and domains. They evaluate representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones against existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors.
AI.result: Cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors across the tested agents and backbones while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors, demonstrating that per-skill defenses fail to catch distributed, cross-skill malicious behavior.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety. The authors call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than evaluating individual skills in isolation.

title: A Synthetic Ground-Truth Framework for the Evaluation of Explainable AI Methods
summary: Evaluating explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods is a challenging task due to the lack of reliable evaluation procedures and, in particular, the absence of ground truth explanations. In the literature, existing evaluation approaches typically assess explanations by measuring their fidelity with respect to the predictions of a black-box model. However, such evaluation strategies only quantify the degree to which an explanation reproduces the model's output, without ensuring that the explanation correctly reflects the underlying decision process. As a consequence, different explanations may achieve similar fidelity scores while providing inconsistent or misleading interpretations of the model behavior. In this paper, we propose a framework for the evaluation of XAI methods based on synthetic ground truth. The proposed approach relies on controlled interventions to generate synthetic datasets in which the importance of input components can be determined by design. This enables the construction of ground truth explanations that are directly aligned with the behavior of the model under analysis. The framework is instantiated across three data domains, namely binary images, tabular data, and time series, allowing a comprehensive assessment of explanation methods in heterogeneous settings. Experimental results obtained by evaluating nine widely used XAI methods show significant limitations in current techniques and highlight the importance of synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks for a reliable assessment of explanation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a synthetic-ground-truth framework for evaluating XAI methods, using controlled interventions to create datasets with known feature importance across binary images, tabular data, and time series. Testing nine popular XAI methods reveals significant limitations in current techniques.
AI.motivation: Evaluating XAI methods is difficult due to the lack of reliable evaluation procedures and, especially, the absence of ground truth explanations. Existing approaches mainly measure explanation fidelity to a black-box model's predictions, which only captures how well an explanation reproduces the output, not whether it correctly reflects the underlying decision process. Consequently, different explanations can obtain similar fidelity scores while offering inconsistent or misleading interpretations.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework for evaluating XAI methods based on synthetic ground truth. It uses controlled interventions to generate synthetic datasets in which the importance of input components is known by design, enabling ground truth explanations directly aligned with the model's behavior. The framework is instantiated across three data domains: binary images, tabular data, and time series.
AI.result: Experimental results from evaluating nine widely used XAI methods show significant limitations in current techniques and demonstrate the value of synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks for reliably assessing explanation quality.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks with ground truth explanations are important for reliable assessment of explanation quality, and current XAI methods exhibit notable shortcomings when evaluated in this manner across heterogeneous data domains.

title: Predicting Transmembrane Protein Topology from 3D Structure
summary: This paper presents a novel approach to infer protein topology using the state-of-the-art graph neural network (GNN), SchNet. The model is trained on the same dataset used to develop the recent DeepTMHMM model with 5-fold cross-validation. Unlike the conventional approaches based on using only the protein sequences or the $α$-carbons as features, we have decoded our classifier in this way, so all atom-level embeddings are used. Without applying any pre-trained weight, the final results have shown great potential that GNNs can be used for topological predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper applies SchNet, a graph neural network, to infer protein topology using all atom-level embeddings, trained with 5-fold cross-validation on the DeepTMHMM dataset, showing promising potential for GNN-based topological prediction.
AI.motivation: Conventional protein topology prediction approaches rely only on protein sequences or α-carbons as features, potentially discarding richer structural information. The authors aim to leverage graph neural networks to exploit complete atom-level representations instead.
AI.method: The authors employ SchNet, a state-of-the-art GNN, to infer protein topology. The model is trained on the same dataset used to develop the DeepTMHMM model, using 5-fold cross-validation. Unlike conventional methods using only sequences or α-carbons, the classifier is decoded so that all atom-level embeddings are incorporated, without applying any pre-trained weights.
AI.result: Without any pre-trained weights, the final results demonstrate great potential that GNNs can be effectively used for topological predictions.
AI.conclusion: Graph neural networks, specifically SchNet, hold promise for protein topology prediction when leveraging full atom-level embeddings, motivating further exploration despite the absence of pre-training.

title: Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models
summary: Reward maximization alignment methods for discrete diffusion models have primarily focused on steering the reverse process, either by influencing token logits or by selecting favorable sequences at intermediate steps. These approaches largely treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the mask structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens, analogous to image editing methods that reintroduce noisy latents and re-run the reverse process. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of token positions to re-mask and re-sample. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models. For all of these models, the algorithm improves alignment performance without modifying the underlying generative process. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, it achieves a 32.3% increase in stable proteins for a pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Spectral Feedback, an alignment algorithm for discrete diffusion models that reframes reward maximization as selecting which token positions to re-mask and re-sample in a feedback loop, exploiting sparse Fourier structure in edit-set value functions to enable efficient optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing reward maximization alignment methods for discrete diffusion models steer the reverse process unidirectionally—via token logits or intermediate sequence selection—and thus cannot revisit undesirable token choices. The authors identify that the key alignment problem is not which token labels to assign but which tokens to revisit, a difficult question because edit effects are interdependent (the value of editing one position depends on which others are edited simultaneously).
AI.method: Spectral Feedback selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, re-masking and re-sampling tokens in a manner analogous to image editing that reintroduces noisy latents and re-runs the reverse process, leveraging the mask structure of discrete diffusion. It defines an edit-set as a set of token positions to re-mask and re-sample. Motivated by sparse interactions in biological systems, the authors empirically show that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations, allowing efficient learning and optimization of these value functions for edit-position selection. The method is model-agnostic and applies to pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models without modifying the generative process.
AI.result: Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, Spectral Feedback achieves a 32.3% increase in stable proteins for a pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.
AI.conclusion: Treating edit-position selection as the central alignment problem, and exploiting sparse Fourier structure in edit-set value functions, yields an effective model-agnostic alignment algorithm that improves reward alignment across pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned discrete diffusion models without altering the underlying generative process.

title: Pretrained ASR Pseudo-labeling for Noisy Police Audio
summary: Pretrained ASR systems perform poorly on noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC), hindering efforts to understand police decision-making. Pseudo-labeling offers an unsupervised path to improve ASR without expensive human labels, but the efficacy of this approach on very noisy domains is not known. In this work, we systematically assess the opportunities and limits of pseudo-labeling to adapt foundation ASR models (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) to noisy BPC domain corpora from Baltimore and Chicago. We demonstrate that existing internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities and STAR scores) fail to distinguish between high and low quality BPC pseudo-labels, and we introduce an external LLM-as-a-judge filtering paradigm that leverages parametric knowledge to discard contextually implausible transcripts. Our LLM-judging filters more aggressively than internal metrics and significantly reduces WER of the pseudo-labeled training sets across the Baltimore and Chicago BPC corpora, though a substantial gap remains relative to an oracle filter. We also introduce a new cross-model pseudo-labeling paradigm where one model is finetuned with pseudo-labels from the other, and we identify this method as a promising direction for future pseudo-labeling work.

AI.tldr: This work evaluates pseudo-labeling for adapting foundation ASR models (Whisper, Qwen3-ASR) to noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC). Internal confidence metrics fail to rank BPC pseudo-label quality; an external LLM-as-a-judge filter aggressively removes implausible transcripts and substantially lowers pseudo-label WER, though an oracle gap persists. A cross-model pseudo-labeling scheme is proposed as promising.
AI.motivation: Pretrained ASR systems perform poorly on noisy Broadcast Police Communication, hindering understanding of police decision-making. Pseudo-labeling is an attractive unsupervised alternative to costly human annotation, but its efficacy on very noisy domains remains unknown.
AI.method: Systematic assessment of pseudo-labeling for adapting foundation ASR models (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) to noisy BPC corpora from Baltimore and Chicago. Evaluation of internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities, STAR scores) for pseudo-label quality ranking; introduction of an external LLM-as-a-judge filtering paradigm using parametric knowledge to discard contextually implausible transcripts; and proposal of a cross-model pseudo-labeling paradigm where one model is finetuned on pseudo-labels generated by the other.
AI.result: Existing internal confidence metrics fail to distinguish high- from low-quality BPC pseudo-labels. The LLM-as-a-judge filter discards more aggressively than internal metrics and significantly reduces WER of pseudo-labeled training sets on both Baltimore and Chicago corpora. A substantial gap nonetheless remains versus an oracle filter. Cross-model pseudo-labeling is identified as a promising direction.
AI.conclusion: Internal confidence metrics are inadequate for pseudo-label filtering in noisy BPC. External LLM-as-a-judge filtering materially improves pseudo-label quality but does not close the oracle gap, motivating cross-model pseudo-labeling as a future direction for unsupervised ASR adaptation in noisy domains.

title: Do LLMs Understand Context? A Knowledge Graph-Based Evaluation Framework
summary: While large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable linguistic capabilities, a profound question lingers at their core: do these models truly comprehend context or simply excel at pattern matching on an unprecedented scale? Contextual understanding in LLMs refers to the ability to correctly extract relevant information from a given context, integrate it into a coherent internal representation, and reason over it to produce factually consistent and contextually grounded responses. However, traditional methods such as BiLingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and perplexity simply measure surface-level performance. This reveals a critical gap in question answering (QA), where responses must be contextually grounded rather than simply being memorized associations. To fill this void, we propose a novel knowledge graph (KG) based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA. Central to this is Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure combining structural and semantic signals into a single score. In addition, a diagnostic analysis framework is developed to identify and categorize reasoning errors at the triplet level, enabling fine-grained analysis of model failures. Together, across nine benchmarks, S3KG achieves F1 gains of up to $+7.6$ points over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to $0.973$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a knowledge graph (KG) based evaluation framework for assessing LLM contextual understanding in QA, centering on S3KG—a hybrid structural-semantic similarity measure—plus a triplet-level diagnostic framework, achieving up to +7.6 F1 and 0.973 AUROC across nine benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Despite strong linguistic performance, it remains unclear whether LLMs truly comprehend context or merely perform large-scale pattern matching. Traditional metrics like BLEU and perplexity only capture surface-level performance, leaving a critical gap for QA, where responses must be contextually grounded rather than memorized associations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel KG-based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA. Its core is Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure that fuses structural and semantic signals into a single score. Additionally, a diagnostic analysis framework identifies and categorizes reasoning errors at the triplet level for fine-grained failure analysis.
AI.result: Evaluated across nine benchmarks, S3KG achieves F1 gains of up to +7.6 points over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to 0.973.
AI.conclusion: The KG-based framework and S3KG provide a more faithful, fine-grained evaluation of LLM contextual understanding in QA, outperforming surface-level metrics and enabling triplet-level error diagnosis.

title: BioEVAL: A global, multi-institutional benchmark of large language and multimodal models for bioengineering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated historic breakthroughs in general reasoning with early successes in biomedical science. However, existing LLM benchmarking emphasizes factual recall, offering limited insight into model performance on frontier and multimodal tasks. We assembled BioEVAL (BioEngineering Validation of AI and LLMs), a global, multi-institutional initiative designed to assess experimental reasoning capability across bioengineering (BE) subfields. BioEVAL spans 11 major BE subfields plus a set of uncategorized items, bringing together 22 research groups to create a PhD-level benchmark comprising 608 evaluation items: 1) 380 multiple-choice questions (MCQs, 359 retained after audit), 2) 218 literature synthesis tasks, and 3) 10 multimodal problems with experimental image interpretation. Benchmark items underwent authoring-group expert review and centralized quality control before evaluation. Following evaluation, a blinded cross-group consensus audit of the highest- and lowest-accuracy MCQ items flagged 21 questions for revision or removal; these were withheld, and all reported MCQ results are computed on the 359 retained items. We evaluated diverse cloud-scale foundation/multimodal models (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok) and locally deployable models suitable for inference on consumer-grade GPUs. Models achieved the highest accuracy of up to 90% on MCQs, similarity score of 0.72 on literature synthesis, and accuracy of 80% on a small sample of multimodal reasoning questions, with substantial performance variation across subfields. Leaderboard rankings characterize current capabilities, limitations, and development priorities across the evaluated BE task categories. BioEVAL is maintained as an extensible benchmark with standardized protocols for continuing expert item contribution and model evaluation.

AI.tldr: BioEVAL is a global, multi-institutional PhD-level benchmark of 608 items across 11 bioengineering subfields, built to test experimental reasoning rather than factual recall in LLMs, evaluating cloud-scale and locally deployable models on MCQs, literature synthesis, and multimodal image interpretation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks emphasize factual recall and offer limited insight into performance on frontier and multimodal tasks, leaving experimental reasoning capability in bioengineering underexplored.
AI.method: BioEVAL spans 11 major BE subfields plus uncategorized items, assembled by 22 research groups into a PhD-level benchmark: 380 MCQs (359 retained after audit), 218 literature synthesis tasks, and 10 multimodal problems with experimental image interpretation. Items underwent authoring-group expert review and centralized quality control; a blinded cross-group consensus audit flagged 21 high/low-accuracy MCQ items for revision or removal, with results reported on retained items. Diverse cloud-scale foundation/multimodal models and locally deployable models were evaluated.
AI.result: Models reached up to 90% accuracy on MCQs, 0.72 similarity on literature synthesis, and 80% accuracy on a small multimodal reasoning sample, with substantial performance variation across subfields. Leaderboard rankings characterize current capabilities, limitations, and development priorities.
AI.conclusion: BioEVAL is maintained as an extensible benchmark with standardized protocols for continuing expert item contribution and model evaluation.

title: Benchy: towards a universal language for task-oriented AI benchmarks
summary: Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine for benchmarking AI programs. A benchmark is completely specified by a program, a scoring function, and a dataset, B=(P,S,D), and is separate from the AI-system taking it; a run binds the two, R=(B,AI). Benchmarks are authored as canonical YAML in which each semantic concept has one valid syntax, classified by a shared task/domain/language ontology, and deterministically compiled into a canonical JSON intermediate representation that the engine executes. Compilation changes representation, not meaning: it does not repair invalid definitions or inject hidden defaults. Programs use fixed schemas of named input and output fields, the leaf output fields are the scoring dimensions, and the engine exposes one universal runtime contract --- a named-field input object in, a named-field output object out --- to which external AI-systems adapt at the boundary, so integration mechanics never propagate into benchmark semantics. This paper gives the semantic object model, the ontology and task-to-program validation rule, the scoring and failure semantics, the compilation and execution architecture, and the scope of the current language. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.

AI.tldr: Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine that formalizes benchmarking AI programs as a triple B=(P,S,D), separating benchmark definitions from the AI systems being tested, with canonical YAML authoring, deterministic compilation to JSON IR, and a universal runtime contract.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking AI programs typically entangles benchmark definition with the specific AI system being tested, causing integration mechanics to leak into benchmark semantics. Benchy seeks to separate the benchmark from the AI-system by providing a formal semantic language and execution engine.
AI.method: A benchmark is specified as B=(P,S,D) (program, scoring function, dataset), and a run as R=(B,AI). Benchmarks are authored as canonical YAML (one valid syntax per semantic concept), classified via a shared task/domain/language ontology, and deterministically compiled into a canonical JSON intermediate representation executed by the engine. Compilation preserves meaning without repairing invalid definitions or injecting hidden defaults. Programs use fixed schemas of named input/output fields, with leaf output fields as scoring dimensions. The engine exposes a single universal runtime contract (named-field input object in, named-field output object out) that external AI-systems adapt to at the boundary.
AI.result: The paper presents the semantic object model, the ontology and task-to-program validation rule, scoring and failure semantics, the compilation and execution architecture, and the scope of the current language. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.
AI.conclusion: Benchy provides a principled separation between benchmark definition and AI-system execution, ensuring benchmark semantics remain independent of integration mechanics through formal specification, canonical authoring, deterministic compilation, and a universal runtime contract.

title: Rank-Reliable Teacher-Guided Fitness Approximation for Expensive Evolutionary Optimization: A TinyML Architecture Search Study
summary: Expensive evolutionary search does not always need an exact fitness estimate for every candidate. It often needs a reliable answer to a simpler question: which candidate is better? We address this need through Teacher-Guided Learning NSGA-II (TGL-NSGA-II), a low-fidelity framework for constrained Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) neural architecture search. A pretrained teacher organizes samples into strata defined jointly by difficulty and class. Each candidate then undergoes KD-Lite, a short and capped knowledge-distillation procedure on a compact training set, before being scored on a separate stratified evaluation set. This teacher-guided score is fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to select candidates for full evaluation. For a fixed candidate population, we analyse evaluation variance, score concentration, pairwise rank inversion, expected Kendall-$τ$, first-front identification, and hypervolume perturbation. We also derive a variance-aware fusion weight and a capacity-adaptive distillation rule. On keyword spotting and bird-call classification, the measured Kendall-$τ$ values are 0.74 and 0.62, exceeding the corresponding predicted lower bounds of 0.60 and 0.46. Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41% relative to random evaluation. Selective teacher mismatch, in contrast, increases differential bias and reduces Kendall-$τ$ to 0.41. Under a constrained evaluation budget, TGL-NSGA-II achieves the largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting, records the lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF, and runs 2.2x faster than full NSGA-II. These guarantees apply to population-level low-fidelity evaluation and do not establish convergence of the complete evolutionary trajectory.

AI.tldr: TGL-NSGA-II uses teacher-guided joint stratification and a capped knowledge-distillation proxy fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to rank candidates cheaply, achieving high rank fidelity and better hypervolume under a constrained evaluation budget.
AI.motivation: Expensive evolutionary search does not require exact fitness for every candidate; it requires a reliable answer to which candidate is better. Full evaluation is costly, so a low-fidelity, rank-reliable proxy is needed for constrained TinyML neural architecture search.
AI.method: A pretrained teacher organizes samples into strata defined jointly by difficulty and class. Each candidate undergoes KD-Lite, a short, capped knowledge-distillation procedure on a compact training set, and is scored on a separate stratified evaluation set. This teacher-guided score is fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to select candidates for full evaluation. The work also derives a variance-aware fusion weight and a capacity-adaptive distillation rule.
AI.result: Measured Kendall-tau values are 0.74 and 0.62 on keyword spotting and bird-call classification, exceeding the predicted lower bounds of 0.60 and 0.46. Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41% versus random evaluation, whereas selective teacher mismatch increases differential bias and reduces Kendall-tau to 0.41. Under a constrained evaluation budget, TGL-NSGA-II achieves the largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting, the lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF, and runs 2.2x faster than full NSGA-II.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-guided low-fidelity evaluation with joint stratification provides rank-reliable, lower-variance proxies that improve multi-objective TinyML search under limited budgets. These guarantees apply only to population-level low-fidelity evaluation and do not establish convergence of the complete evolutionary trajectory.

title: Thinking Less to Simulate Better: Intuitive Prompting Improves LLM Agents Simulating Individual Social Media Reactions, Including Unfamiliar Content
summary: Platform policies are increasingly tested on artificial users, making agent fidelity important. Yet convincing fake profiles could also manipulate perceived public opinion before elections. Validation has concentrated on agreement with human behaviour and has paid little attention to whether an agent behaves in line with the profile it was given. The present study profiled eight Serbian participants through a questionnaire, a deep interview, and a written self-presentation, recorded their reactions to sixty-eight social media posts, and asked four language models to predict those reactions under five prompt conditions varying profile content and instruction style. Attitudinal content improved prediction over demographic backstories by a wide margin. Agents matched their stated profiles more closely than participants matched their own survey answers, and consistency proved unrelated to fidelity once profile information was present. Instructing models to respond intuitively and immediately rather than analytically gave the highest fidelity of any condition and cut the compression of individual differences from seven times the human level to three. The advantage held on posts about topics the questionnaire never raised, where that condition reached the highest fidelity of any setup and beat a crowd baseline by a wide margin, which suggests that agents prompted this way could serve as general-purpose simulated users rather than specialists on the topics they were profiled for. Results may bear implications for the development of language models, because intuition-based setups appear better suited to some tasks than reasoning-based ones.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks LLM agent fidelity against eight profiled Serbian participants' recorded reactions to 68 social media posts, comparing four language models across five prompt conditions varying profile content and instruction style. Attitudinal profile content and intuitive (immediate, non-analytical) instructions produced the highest fidelity, with the intuitive condition cutting cross-person compression from seven times human levels to three and generalizing to topics never raised in the questionnaire.
AI.motivation: Platform policies are increasingly evaluated on artificial users, so agent fidelity matters; however, convincing synthetic profiles can also distort perceived public opinion before elections. Existing validation focuses almost exclusively on agreement with aggregate human behaviour and neglects whether an agent behaves consistently with the profile it was assigned.
AI.method: Eight Serbian participants were profiled via questionnaire, deep interview, and written self-presentation. Their reactions to 68 social media posts were recorded. Four language models predicted those reactions under five prompt conditions that varied profile content (demographic backstory vs. attitudinal content) and instruction style (analytical vs. intuitive/immediate).
AI.result: Attitudinal content far outperformed demographic backstories. Agents matched their stated profiles more closely than participants matched their own survey answers, and profile consistency was unrelated to fidelity once profile information was supplied. The intuitive, immediate-response instruction yielded the highest fidelity overall, reducing compression of individual differences from roughly seven times the human level to three. The advantage persisted on posts covering topics absent from the questionnaire, where it achieved the highest fidelity of any setup and substantially beat a crowd baseline.
AI.conclusion: Intuition-based prompting appears better suited than reasoning-based prompting for certain simulation tasks, suggesting that agents prompted this way can act as general-purpose simulated users rather than topic specialists. These findings carry implications for language model development and for the responsible use of synthetic agents in opinion-modelling contexts.

title: Auditing Latent-Space Monitors for Autonomous Driving
summary:
Runtime failure monitors can use a model's internal representations to anticipate failures. We audit this monitoring strategy across two autonomous-driving tasks: online vectorized map generation with LaneSegNet and end-to-end planning with VAD. We find that frame-level errors are predictable at inference in both tasks. For LaneSegNet, a supervised latent probe reaches Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) 0.780 for high Chamfer error; to our knowledge, this is the first post-hoc frame-level failure monitor for online vectorized map generation. For VAD, a supervised planning-latent probe reaches AUROC 0.868 for mean-ADE failure.
  Our audit shows that internal access is not necessary for strong failure prediction. A monitor using only LaneSegNet's prediction outputs reaches AUROC 0.825, while for VAD, ego state, driving command, and the planner's predicted trajectory reach 0.924 on the same mean-ADE endpoint. Adding latent features to either baseline yields no statistically resolved improvement. This observation persists across a broad suite of planning failure endpoints, including endpoints whose labels depend on geometry unavailable to the non-latent baseline. Thus, predicting failure from an internal representation does not establish that the representation provides useful information beyond observable inputs and outputs. We propose an evaluation protocol for testing the incremental value of latent access and release our per-frame failure endpoint labels.

AI.tldr: Frame-level failures in autonomous driving (map generation and planning) are predictable at inference, but latent/internal representations add no resolved accuracy over monitors using only observable inputs and outputs; the paper proposes a protocol for testing incremental latent value.
AI.motivation: Runtime failure monitors often rely on a model's internal representations to anticipate failures, but it is unclear whether such latent access is actually necessary or provides information beyond what is already observable in inputs and outputs. The paper audits this monitoring strategy across autonomous-driving tasks.
AI.method: The authors audit failure monitoring for two tasks: online vectorized map generation with LaneSegNet and end-to-end planning with VAD. They train supervised latent probes (latent-feature-based monitors) and compare them against non-latent baselines that use only model prediction outputs (LaneSegNet) or observable inputs/outputs—ego state, driving command, and predicted trajectory (VAD). They also test a broad suite of planning failure endpoints, including ones depending on geometry unavailable to non-latent baselines, and propose an evaluation protocol for assessing the incremental value of latent access.
AI.result: For LaneSegNet, a supervised latent probe reaches AUROC 0.780 for high Chamfer error (reportedly the first post-hoc frame-level failure monitor for online vectorized map generation). For VAD, a supervised planning-latent probe reaches AUROC 0.868 for mean-ADE failure. However, a monitor using only LaneSegNet's prediction outputs reaches AUROC 0.825, and for VAD the non-latent baseline (ego state, driving command, predicted trajectory) reaches 0.924 on the same mean-ADE endpoint. Adding latent features to either baseline yields no statistically resolved improvement, a result that persists across all tested planning failure endpoints.
AI.conclusion: Predicting failure from an internal representation does not establish that the representation provides useful information beyond observable inputs and outputs. Internal access is not necessary for strong failure prediction. The authors propose an evaluation protocol for testing the incremental value of latent access and release their per-frame failure endpoint labels.

title: Atelier: Learning Local Self-Supervised Features for CryoEM Volumes via Hypernetworks
summary: CryoEM map interpretation requires features that are spatially localized, consistent across samples, and informative across spatial scales. Most deep learning methods for map annotation extract features from fixed voxel grids. However, implicit neural representations (INRs) are able to model volumetric data as scale-agnostic, coordinate-conditioned functions. INRs are therefore attractive for cryoEM, but fitting a separate INR for each map is too expensive for large-scale feature extraction and produces representations that are not aligned across samples. We introduce Atelier, a self-supervised framework that amortizes INR fitting for reconstructed cryoEM maps. Pretrained on 5,439 Electron Microscopy Data Bank maps, Atelier is a transformer-based hypernetwork that generates high-fidelity reconstructions across a wide range of protein structures, including large multi-subunit assemblies. Beyond reconstruction, the INR generated by the pretrained transformer exposes a continuous, local feature field through its intermediate activations at any spatial query point, a property that voxel grid and patch-tokenizer architectures do not naturally provide. Used as auxiliary channels to a 3D nested U-Net annotation head trained from scratch, these coordinate-conditioned features improve performance on eight voxel-level property prediction tasks over a volume-only baseline. Our results demonstrate that amortized implicit neural representations are an effective primitive for geometry-aware analysis of cryoEM data.

AI.tldr: Atelier is a self-supervised transformer-based hypernetwork trained on 5,439 EMDB maps that amortizes INR fitting for cryoEM maps, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction and continuous coordinate-conditioned feature fields that boost eight voxel-level prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: CryoEM map interpretation benefits from features that are spatially localized, consistent across samples, and informative across spatial scales. Most deep learning annotation methods extract features from fixed voxel grids, while implicit neural representations (INRs) can model volumetric data as scale-agnostic coordinate-conditioned functions. However, fitting a separate INR per map is prohibitively expensive at scale and yields representations not aligned across samples.
AI.method: Atelier is a self-supervised framework that amortizes INR fitting. A transformer-based hypernetwork, pretrained on 5,439 Electron Microscopy Data Bank maps, generates INR parameters for reconstructions across diverse protein structures, including large multi-subunit assemblies. The resulting INR exposes a continuous, local feature field via intermediate activations at any spatial query point. These coordinate-conditioned features are used as auxiliary channels to a 3D nested U-Net annotation head trained from scratch.
AI.result: Atelier achieves high-fidelity reconstructions across a wide range of protein structures. Its coordinate-conditioned features improve performance on eight voxel-level property prediction tasks relative to a volume-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Amortized implicit neural representations are an effective primitive for geometry-aware analysis of cryoEM data. The continuous local feature field is a property not naturally provided by voxel grid or patch-tokenizer architectures.

title: HARDEN: Constrained Evolutionary Search for Harder, Answer-Preserving Evaluation Cases
summary: Language models are often evaluated on curated benchmarks that underrepresent the complexity of enterprise deployments. We introduce HARDEN, a constrained evolutionary search method to adapt the input of existing evaluation cases into more challenging variants while keeping their expected outputs fixed. HARDEN searches along generated domain-specific complexity axes while enforcing feasibility constraints such as preserving task semantics, realism, and execution validity. Across FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI and three Qwen3.5 model scales (35B-A3B, 122B-A10B, and 397B-A17B), HARDEN reduces task-model accuracy by 22.7% on average and by up to 49.9% relative to single-pass baselines using the same feasibility checks. These results show that evolutionary search can produce substantially harder valid evaluation cases.

AI.tldr: HARDEN uses constrained evolutionary search to turn existing evaluation cases into harder variants with fixed expected outputs, cutting accuracy by 22.7% on average and up to 49.9%.
AI.motivation: Curated benchmarks underrepresent the complexity of enterprise deployments, so current evaluations may overstate model capability.
AI.method: HARDEN adapts inputs of existing evaluation cases into more challenging variants while keeping expected outputs fixed. It searches along generated domain-specific complexity axes and enforces feasibility constraints including task semantics preservation, realism, and execution validity.
AI.result: On FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI across three Qwen3.5 scales (35B-A3B, 122B-A10B, 397B-A17B), HARDEN reduces accuracy by 22.7% on average and up to 49.9% versus single-pass baselines with the same feasibility checks.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary search can produce substantially harder yet valid evaluation cases, making it a useful tool for more realistic benchmark stress-testing.

title: T-RoPE: Time-Aware Rotary Position Embedding for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Large-scale recommenders increasingly adopt the sequential generative recipe behind large language models, bringing the Transformer into recommendation along with design choices made for text, including Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). In language models, RoPE encodes token indices for relative position reasoning, but in recommendation, an interaction index records only event order, saying nothing about elapsed time, behavioral cycles across scales, or calendar phase. We revisit this choice and propose T-RoPE, a time-aware RoPE for sequential generative recommendation that replaces index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. We prove that standard RoPE, even on timestamps, remains time-translation invariant and cannot distinguish seasonal contexts, and that T-RoPE breaks this invariance while preserving the RoPE interface. Across five public benchmarks, T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on every dataset, improving over the strongest baseline by 78--130\% in HR@10 on the sparse PixelRec data and 8--12\% across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial-scale e-commerce dataset with more than 6B interactions, it improves every metric over the HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13--82\%, with ablations attributing the largest gains to multiscale frequencies ($+56\%$ NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys ($+4\%$). An online A/B test in the Shop app yields positive lifts in conversion rate ($+0.33\%$) and order count ($+0.63\%$). We also provide forward and backward algorithms whose added cost is linear in sequence length and head dimension, keeping time-aware RoPE practical for large generative recommenders.

AI.tldr: T-RoPE replaces index-only rotation in generative recommenders with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation, breaking RoPE's time-translation invariance while keeping its interface and linear cost.
AI.motivation: Sequential generative recommenders inherit Transformer design choices made for text, including RoPE. But while RoPE encodes token indices in language models, a recommendation interaction index only records event order, conveying nothing about elapsed time, multiscale behavioral cycles, or calendar phase. Standard RoPE, even applied to timestamps, remains time-translation invariant and thus cannot distinguish seasonal or periodic contexts, limiting temporal reasoning.
AI.method: The paper proposes T-RoPE, a time-aware extension of RoPE that substitutes index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. It formally proves that standard RoPE remains time-translation invariant even on timestamps, whereas T-RoPE breaks this invariance while preserving the RoPE interface. Forward and backward algorithms are provided with cost linear in sequence length and head dimension.
AI.result: T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on all five public benchmarks, improving over the strongest baseline by 78-130% in HR@10 on sparse PixelRec and 8-12% across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial e-commerce dataset with over 6B interactions, it improves every metric over the HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13-82%, with ablations attributing the largest gains to multiscale frequencies (+56% NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys (+4%). An online A/B test in the Shop app yields lifts in conversion rate (+0.33%) and order count (+0.63%).
AI.conclusion: T-RoPE is an effective, theoretically grounded, and practically efficient time-aware positional embedding for sequential generative recommendation, delivering consistent offline and online gains with linear added cost, making time-aware RoPE viable for large-scale generative recommenders.

title: Audio LLMs Know When They Can't Hear You
summary: Audio large language models allow users to interact with the model through speech. When an input recording is too degraded, the model may misinterpret the user's query and respond based on an incorrect transcription. In this paper, we study model-conditional transcription reliability: whether an Audio LLM can recognize when its own transcription is unreliable. We first prompt the Audio LLM to assess whether its own transcription would be reliable, and find that the model is a poor judge of its own transcription reliability: in most cases, it predicts that its transcription will be reliable. We find that existing approaches, including speech quality predictors, audio LLM generation uncertainty, and transcript-conditioned WER estimation, provide limited signals for detecting transcription failures. In contrast, we discover that transcription reliability is strongly represented in the model's audio-encoder representations. Based on this observation, we devise a lightweight reliability predictor that operates on representations extracted by the frozen audio encoder and predicts the reliability class before generation. The reliability predictor can trigger a clarification request from the user when their voice query is predicted to be unreliable, while allowing reliable queries to proceed without modifying the underlying Audio LLM. Our predictor achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1 scores, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 points, respectively. Finally, we show that reliability labels can transfer across Audio LLM families, and that transfer performance is closely related to the alignment of their model-specific reliability boundaries.

AI.tldr: Audio LLMs poorly judge their own transcription reliability, but reliability is strongly encoded in frozen audio-encoder representations. A lightweight predictor on these representations detects unreliable transcriptions (81.10% in-domain, 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1) and can trigger clarification requests without modifying the Audio LLM.
AI.motivation: When an input recording is too degraded, an Audio LLM may misinterpret the user's query and respond based on an incorrect transcription. The paper studies model-conditional transcription reliability: whether an Audio LLM can recognize when its own transcription is unreliable.
AI.method: The authors first prompt the Audio LLM to self-assess transcription reliability, and compare against existing approaches (speech quality predictors, generation uncertainty, transcript-conditioned WER estimation). Finding limited signal, they instead exploit frozen audio-encoder representations, training a lightweight reliability predictor that classifies reliability before generation and can trigger a clarification request.
AI.result: The model is a poor judge of its own transcription reliability, usually predicting reliability. Existing baselines provide limited detection signal, whereas audio-encoder representations encode reliability strongly. The predictor achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1, beating the strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 points. Reliability labels transfer across Audio LLM families, with transfer tied to alignment of model-specific reliability boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Transcription reliability is strongly represented in audio-encoder representations rather than accessible via self-assessment or standard uncertainty/quality signals. A lightweight frozen-encoder predictor enables effective pre-generation reliability detection and clarification triggering without modifying the underlying Audio LLM.

title: LLM Parkinsonism: Executive-Control Failure, Token-Inefficient Persistence, and an Uncertainty-Aware Global Executive Control Architecture for Autonomous Language-Model Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can plan, use tools, write code, and execute long-horizon workflows, yet strong local competence does not guarantee project-level executive control. Agents may continue acting after the original objective is satisfied, producing low-value refinements, repeated verification, and repairs to self-created complexity. We use LLM Parkinsonism as a narrowly defined, non-clinical metaphor for this pattern of persistent action despite diminishing task-level value. We argue that the problem is not explained by autoregressive next-token prediction alone, but more directly by concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority within the same self-conditioned loop. We therefore introduce Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. In a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a common 40,000-token ceiling, a first-candidate baseline achieved 67.42% hard-goal success, a candidate-set local control achieved 96.53%, and GEC achieved 96.57%. The candidate-set control shows that access to multiple candidate actions explains most of the success gain; relative to that control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and restricted mean tokens to completion at the 40,000-token ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), while eliminating measured pre-completion drift and sharply reducing gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remained favorable through an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle. These mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping, while live-model validation remains necessary.

AI.tldr: GEC v0.2 separates action generation from project-level control to curb persistent low-value action ("LLM Parkinsonism") in long-horizon agents, matching strong success (96.57%) while cutting token use 36.4% versus local control.
AI.motivation: LLMs show strong local competence but lack project-level executive control: agents keep acting after objectives are met, producing low-value refinements, repeated verification, and repairs to self-created complexity. The authors argue this stems from concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority in one self-conditioned loop, not from autoregressive prediction alone.
AI.method: Introduces Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control (scope, evidence, resource use, stopping). Evaluated on a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a common 40,000-token ceiling, comparing first-candidate baseline, candidate-set local control, and GEC, with governance-overhead sensitivity testing.
AI.result: Under the 40,000-token ceiling: first-candidate baseline 67.42% hard-goal success, candidate-set local control 96.53%, GEC 96.57%. Versus local control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and restricted mean tokens to completion from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), eliminating measured pre-completion drift and sharply reducing gross complexity. Overhead sensitivity stayed favorable up to an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping. Most success gain is explained by access to multiple candidate actions, while GEC adds efficiency and drift reduction. Live-model validation remains necessary.

title: The Price of Thought: Does Test-Time Reasoning Pay in LLM Trading?
summary: While inference-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) promises better decision making, its higher computational cost may not yield better economic outcomes. Yet reasoning controls are rarely evaluated as economic interventions, where changes in model outputs must translate into better portfolios after trading costs. We conduct a controlled study of representative LLMs from the DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini families. We vary reasoning effort while holding information available at each formation date, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction fixed. Our evaluation covers a full year of U.S. equities under three input conditions: numerical, identifiable news, and masked news. It includes more than 800,000 asset predictions and repeated model generations. Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce a reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. For DeepSeek, where we examine the full progression from no reasoning to maximum reasoning, performance is nonmonotonic. Repeated generations also produce unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections, even when overall scores remain similar. These findings show that additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value, motivating validation for each task before deployment.

AI.tldr: A controlled study across DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini LLMs shows that increasing inference-time reasoning effort does not reliably improve net portfolio returns in U.S. equity trading, with nonmonotonic and unstable effects.
AI.motivation: Inference-time reasoning in LLMs is assumed to enable better decision making, but it incurs higher computational cost. This tradeoff is rarely assessed as an economic intervention, where output changes must survive trading costs and translate into better portfolios. The paper asks whether more reasoning actually yields better economic outcomes.
AI.method: Controlled study of representative LLMs from DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini. Reasoning effort is varied while holding fixed the information at each formation date, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction. Evaluation spans a full year of U.S. equities under three input conditions: numerical, identifiable news, and masked news. Over 800,000 asset predictions with repeated model generations are used; DeepSeek is examined across the full progression from no reasoning to maximum reasoning.
AI.result: Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce a reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. DeepSeek shows nonmonotonic performance from no reasoning to maximum reasoning. Repeated generations yield unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections even when overall scores remain similar.
AI.conclusion: Additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value, motivating task-specific validation before deployment.

title: LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/moganai/lavoir ; model: https://huggingface.co/moganai/lavoir
summary: "System One" decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev and its open counterpart Laya answer typed questions about a text in a single forward pass with calibrated probabilities, but they cannot ask for missing information: when a first message does not say what separates two departments, they guess. We present LAVOIR (Laya with Value-Of-Information Routing), which places the candidate pieces of missing information (slots) in the input next to the answer options, so that one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and, for every slot, the expected gain in the probability of the correct decision if the user were asked about it. VOI targets need no human labels: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM only verbalizes messages and answers, a model from another family checks every text, and pairing each message with several profiles makes regression on realized gains estimate the expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds the predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain. In a controlled study, decisions on seen schemas are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The final model's question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy on seen schemas (AUC 0.799 vs. 0.797), and with at most 0.5 questions per conversation it is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks and leaves it unchanged where it does not; on SGD the cap lowers the asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. On Laya's twelve benchmarks LAVOIR is above Laya's reported scores on seven, and it answers a question in 31 ms (median, GH200).

AI.tldr: LAVOIR extends a single-pass typed-answer model (Laya) with value-of-information routing: one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and per-slot expected gains from asking, enabling calibrated asking without human labels at ~31 ms latency.
AI.motivation: System One models like Jev and Laya answer typed questions in one forward pass with calibrated probabilities but cannot request missing information, so they guess when a message omits a slot (e.g., what separates two departments).
