The paper aims to add targeted, value-of-information-driven question asking to such single-pass models without requiring human labels for VOI targets.
AI.method: LAVOIR places candidate missing-information slots in the input alongside the answer options, so one forward pass yields both the decision distribution and, per slot, the expected gain in the probability of the correct decision if the user were asked. VOI targets are label-free: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM only verbalizes messages and answers, a model from a different family verifies every text, and each message is paired with several profiles so regression on realized gains estimates expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain.
AI.result: On seen schemas, decisions are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The final model's question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy (AUC 0.799 vs. 0.797); with at most 0.5 questions per conversation it is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks and leaves it unchanged where it does not; on SGD the cap lowers the asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. On Laya's twelve benchmarks LAVOIR exceeds Laya's reported scores on seven, answering in 31 ms median (GH200).
AI.conclusion: A single forward pass can jointly produce calibrated decisions and per-slot value-of-information estimates, letting a System One model ask only when asking is worthwhile. The label-free construction and Gini-impurity cap yield near-oracle question policies, measurable real-conversation gains, a much lower asking rate, and competitive benchmark scores at low latency.

title: CRC-Router: Risk-Constrained Routing for Medical Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored in medical imaging to improve throughput and reduce clinician workload; however, safe deployment remains challenging because autonomous errors may propagate into downstream clinical decisions. A central requirement is therefore not only strong predictive performance, but also a reliable routing mechanism that determines when the system should proceed autonomously and when a case should be escalated for further review. To address this gap, we propose CRC-Router, a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module that is applicable to both conventional medical prediction models and agentic medical AI systems. CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with the predictive score to construct a per-finding routing feature vector, maps this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model, and then applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under a user-specified risk target. Instantiated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk--coverage trade-off among the evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module integrated with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent. These results demonstrate both the effectiveness of CRC-Router in selective medical automation and its modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/CRC-Router

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CRC-Router, a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module that decides when a medical imaging AI system can act autonomously and when to escalate cases, achieving a strong risk-coverage trade-off on chest X-ray triage.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems in medical imaging aim to improve throughput and reduce clinician workload, but autonomous errors can propagate into downstream clinical decisions. Therefore, beyond strong predictive performance, a reliable routing mechanism is needed to determine when the system should proceed autonomously and when a case should be escalated for further review.
AI.method: CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with the predictive score to build a per-finding routing feature vector, maps this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk via a lightweight per-finding risk model, and applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under a user-specified risk target. It is model-agnostic, applicable to conventional prediction models and agentic systems.
AI.result: Instantiated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage with the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk-coverage trade-off among evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent.
AI.conclusion: CRC-Router is effective for selective medical automation and offers modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/CRC-Router.

title: Analyzing and Mitigating Cost-Inefficient Behaviors in Coding Agents
summary: Although effective, coding agents often incur substantial monetary costs. Their recurring cost-inefficient behaviors remain underexplored. We conduct the first study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents, analyzing 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified. We identify three cost-inefficient behaviors: subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, and test re-execution. We then evaluate three mitigation strategies: structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, and developer-designed skills, over 10k trajectories on held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks. Our main findings are: (1) The three behaviors affect 79.00\%--98.00\% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75\% of task cost. (2) Structure-aware retrieval can introduce retrieval overhead and alter agent delegation, causing inconsistent improvements in retrieval efficiency and cost increases of up to 28.14\%. (3) Agent-synthesized skills tend to produce low-level, trace-specific guidance, limiting their effectiveness and generality. (4) In contrast, developer-designed skills provide high-level, trace-agnostic guidance, reducing cost by up to 41.73\%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents. Analyzing 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent on SWE-bench Verified, it identifies three recurring cost-inefficient behaviors and evaluates three mitigation strategies over 10k trajectories, finding that developer-designed skills reduce cost by up to 41.73%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are effective but incur substantial monetary costs, and their recurring cost-inefficient behaviors remain underexplored. Existing work has not systematically characterized or mitigated these behavioral inefficiencies.
AI.method: The authors conduct the first study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents, analyzing 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified. They identify three cost-inefficient behaviors: subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, and test re-execution. They then evaluate three mitigation strategies—structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, and developer-designed skills—over 10k trajectories on held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks.
AI.result: Three behaviors affect 79.00%–98.00% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75% of task cost. Structure-aware retrieval can introduce retrieval overhead and alter agent delegation, causing inconsistent retrieval-efficiency improvements and cost increases up to 28.14%. Agent-synthesized skills yield low-level, trace-specific guidance with limited effectiveness and generality, whereas developer-designed skills provide high-level, trace-agnostic guidance, reducing cost by up to 41.73%—roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral cost inefficiencies are pervasive yet underexplored in coding agents. Among the mitigation strategies studied, developer-designed skills are the most effective, offering trace-agnostic guidance that substantially outperforms agent-synthesized skills and structure-aware retrieval.

title: Learning What to Skip: Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Multi-agent LLM workflows use planning, execution, verification, and summarization to improve task performance, yet the value of each component depends on the state already produced. Executing every component can waste computation or overwrite a correct intermediate answer. We formulate component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: full-workflow logs reveal the executed trajectory's reward, while controlled skip interventions reveal the consequences of omitting a future step. We introduce Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. When an early skip is rejected, the controller can continue execution and reconsider a later component. Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy in the evaluated settings. Scale-up and second-topology experiments further examine component redundancy, while shared-error cases reveal why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection. These findings connect efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components.

AI.tldr: LW2S frames skipping multi-agent LLM workflow components as counterfactual credit assignment, learning action-specific safety models from skip interventions and using calibrated guards to reduce token cost while matching or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM workflows (planning, execution, verification, summarization) improve task performance, but the value of each component depends on the state already produced. Running every component can waste computation or overwrite a correct intermediate answer, so deciding when to omit components is the key challenge.
AI.method: The paper formulates component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: full-workflow logs give the executed trajectory's reward, while controlled skip interventions reveal the consequences of omitting a future step. It introduces Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. If an early skip is rejected, the controller continues execution and reconsiders a later component.
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy. Scale-up and second-topology experiments examine component redundancy, and shared-error cases show why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection.
AI.conclusion: The findings link efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components, indicating that selective skipping via counterfactual safety modeling is a viable route to cheaper multi-agent LLM workflows.

title: From S3Q Theory to Implementation: Towards an Architecture for Machine Qualia
summary: A key challenge in machine consciousness research is translating theoretical models into computational-level implementations. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing a five-layer implementation architecture for the S3Q (Simulated, Situated, Structurally Coherent) theory of consciousness. Rather than introducing novel formalisms, the architecture composes published computational primitives into a single pipeline. S3Q identifies three jointly necessary conditions for qualia: (1) grounded sensorimotor situatedness, (2) internal simulation via a world model, and (3) structural coherence between predictions and observations. No existing computational system implements all three simultaneously. We map each S3Q tenet to specific, compatible computational machinery and specify how these components interface within a single representation pipeline that operates on continuous, differentiable, per-object slot vectors, along with a developmental bootstrap sequence and falsifiable predictions for the composed system that no subset of the architecture produces in isolation. The model suggests that a basic sense of "self" develops by linking actions to their outcomes, and that behavior falls into three patterns (hesitation, curiosity, or avoidance) depending on how unexpected an outcome is and whether it is experienced as positive or negative. Each prediction is individually falsifiable, providing the field with a testable framework to advance our understanding of machine consciousness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a five-layer implementation architecture for the S3Q theory of consciousness, composing existing computational primitives into a single pipeline that realizes three jointly necessary conditions for qualia and yields falsifiable predictions.
AI.motivation: Machine consciousness research struggles to translate theoretical models into computational-level implementations. The S3Q (Simulated, Situated, Structurally Coherent) theory specifies three jointly necessary conditions for qualia, but no existing computational system implements all three simultaneously, leaving the theory untestable at the implementation level.
AI.method: Rather than introducing novel formalisms, the authors compose published computational primitives into a five-layer pipeline. They map each S3Q tenet to compatible machinery: grounded sensorimotor situatedness (condition 1), internal simulation via a world model (condition 2), and structural coherence between predictions and observations (condition 3). Components interface within a single representation pipeline operating on continuous, differentiable, per-object slot vectors, supplemented by a developmental bootstrap sequence and falsifiable predictions.
AI.result: The composed architecture suggests a basic sense of "self" develops by linking actions to their outcomes, and that behavior falls into three patterns—hesitation, curiosity, or avoidance—depending on how unexpected an outcome is and whether it is experienced as positive or negative. The system yields predictions that no subset of the architecture produces in isolation.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides the field with a testable framework for machine consciousness, where each prediction is individually falsifiable, advancing understanding of how theoretical models can be realized computationally.

title: ORCA: Evaluating LLMs on Data Science Code Translation
summary: Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) is the process of converting code between data science libraries while preserving functional equivalence and enabling interoperability across data science ecosystems. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable progress in Data Science Code Generation (DSCG), their performance in DSCT remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce ORCA, a comprehensive benchmark with two complementary settings: ORCA-MAIN, which comprises 1,600 carefully curated grounding-level tasks across 3 representative domains: Data Querying, Data Manipulation, and Deep Learning; and ORCA-PROJECT, which contains 200 translation tasks over complete data science projects across 7 data science task types. Each task is accompanied by annotated reference translations and test cases for validating functional equivalence. We further incorporate a multi-stage quality verification process that thoroughly verifies task correctness and test case robustness. Experimental results demonstrate challenges in DSCT, with even frontier LLMs showing limited performance. Specifically, Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves a success rate of 56.92% on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT, indicating considerable room for improvement in DSCT. We also observe a clear directional preference in DSCT, where translation is consistently easier when the source code expresses the task through more explicit, fine-grained operations. Motivated by this, we propose an intent-augmented method, in which the model first infers source-code intent and then uses it as additional context for translation, achieving average absolute success-rate gains of 4.80% and 5.33% on ORCA-MAIN and ORCA-PROJECT, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ORCA, a benchmark for Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) with 1,600 grounding-level tasks (ORCA-MAIN) and 200 project-level tasks (ORCA-PROJECT), revealing that even frontier LLMs perform poorly, and proposes an intent-augmented method that improves success rates.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown progress in Data Science Code Generation (DSCG), but their ability to translate code between data science libraries (DSCT) remains insufficiently studied. The authors identify this gap and aim to systematically evaluate and improve LLMs on DSCT.
AI.method: The authors build the ORCA benchmark with two settings: ORCA-MAIN (1,600 grounding-level tasks spanning Data Querying, Data Manipulation, and Deep Learning) and ORCA-PROJECT (200 translation tasks over complete data science projects across 7 task types). Each task includes annotated reference translations and test cases for validating functional equivalence, plus a multi-stage quality verification process. They also propose an intent-augmented method where the model first infers source-code intent, then uses it as additional context for translation.
AI.result: Even frontier LLMs show limited performance: Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves 56.92% success on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT. A clear directional preference is observed, with translation being easier when source code uses more explicit, fine-grained operations. The intent-augmented method yields average absolute success-rate gains of 4.80% (ORCA-MAIN) and 5.33% (ORCA-PROJECT).
AI.conclusion: DSCT remains challenging for current LLMs, leaving considerable room for improvement. The observed directional preference motivates intent-augmented translation, which improves performance, highlighting source-code intent modeling as a promising direction.

title: Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing for Robust Pairwise LLM Judging
summary: Pairwise language-model judges can gather evidence through direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification, but no single protocol is best across benchmarks and judge backbones. We introduce Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing (BAER), which adapts the evidence mechanism while preserving candidate symmetry: swapping the two responses may reverse the preference but cannot change its strength. BAER separates each expert's signed preference from candidate-invariant reliability and builds three symmetric heads: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. Development data select one head for each benchmark--backbone condition, and that choice is frozen before testing. Across four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones, BAER achieves the highest test accuracy among the compared methods in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87--7.32 points over the strongest external baseline. The results show that adapting how evidence is gathered is more reliable than fixing one judging protocol everywhere.

AI.tldr: BAER adapts the evidence-gathering mechanism of pairwise LLM judges while preserving candidate symmetry, selecting one of three symmetric heads per benchmark-backbone condition and achieving top accuracy in all eight settings.
AI.motivation: No single pairwise judging protocol (direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification) is best across all benchmarks and judge backbones, so fixing one protocol everywhere is suboptimal.
AI.method: BAER separates each expert's signed preference from candidate-invariant reliability and builds three symmetric heads: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. It preserves candidate symmetry (swapping responses may reverse preference but not its strength). Development data select one head per benchmark-backbone condition, frozen before testing.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones, BAER achieves the highest test accuracy in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87-7.32 points over the strongest external baseline.
AI.conclusion: Adapting how evidence is gathered is more reliable than fixing a single judging protocol everywhere, and doing so under a symmetry-preserving design yields consistent gains.

title: Selective Amortization of Full-Budget Counterfactual Reasoning for Visual Token Communication
comment: Visual token communication, counterfactual evaluation, selective computation, knowledge distillation, resource allocation
summary: Generative image communication transmits compact semantic tokens under a limited packet budget, where token selection directly affects the final reconstruction quality after the complete packet is decoded. However, accurately estimating the terminal value of every candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstruction, resulting in substantial encoder-side computation. To address this problem, we propose ACV-Gate, an adaptive candidate evaluation framework that learns to approximate full-budget counterfactual evaluation and selectively assigns exact evaluations to the most informative candidates. Specifically, a set-aware student is trained using terminal advantages and regrets to predict candidate rankings directly, while a selective refinement mechanism evaluates only a bounded candidate set containing both Local-MDL and direct actions; cost-based thresholds further enable explicit control of the average evaluation workload. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show that ACV-Gate consistently improves reconstruction quality while substantially reducing candidate evaluations; at 0.20 bpp, the primary adaptive configuration improves PSNR over LocalMDL by 0.636 dB with only 2.13 candidate evaluations per image, corresponding to 27.60% of the calls required by the Exact-Full expert. Matched-candidate comparisons, synchronized GPU measurements, and evaluations on STL-10 and 384 *384 scale transfer further demonstrate consistent quality computation trade-offs, with particularly pronounced gains at low bit rates. These results show that combining terminal-value learning with selective candidate evaluation provides an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication.

AI.tldr: ACV-Gate learns to predict token candidate rankings via terminal advantages/regrets and selectively applies exact evaluations, improving reconstruction quality while cutting encoder-side candidate evaluations under a packet budget.
AI.motivation: In packet-constrained generative image communication, token selection determines final reconstruction quality after full packet decoding. Accurately estimating the terminal value of every candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstruction, causing substantial encoder-side computation. A method is needed to reduce this expensive counterfactual evaluation without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: ACV-Gate is an adaptive candidate evaluation framework that approximates full-budget counterfactual evaluation. A set-aware student model is trained with terminal advantages and regrets to directly predict candidate rankings. A selective refinement mechanism then evaluates only a bounded candidate set containing Local-MDL and direct actions, and cost-based thresholds explicitly control the average evaluation workload.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, ACV-Gate consistently improves reconstruction quality while greatly reducing candidate evaluations. At 0.20 bpp, the primary adaptive configuration improves PSNR over LocalMDL by 0.636 dB using only 2.13 candidate evaluations per image, i.e., 27.60% of the calls required by the Exact-Full expert. Matched-candidate comparisons, synchronized GPU measurements, and evaluations on STL-10 and 384x384 scale transfer confirm consistent quality-computation trade-offs, with the largest gains at low bit rates.
AI.conclusion: Combining terminal-value learning with selective candidate evaluation offers an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication, achieving better reconstruction quality at substantially lower evaluation cost.

title: Anatomy-Aware Dexterity-Driven Design Optimization of Surgical Continuum Robots
summary: Performing complex medical procedures with continuum robots requires careful selection of their geometric design parameters. The robot should have high dexterity in the specific anatomical environment of its procedure. This work presents a design optimization method that considers both dexterity and anatomy. We introduce the Reachable Volumetric Dexterous Solid Angle (RVDSA) metric as our objective, which measures the ability of a robot's end effector to reach the points in a goal volume from different directions via collision-free paths from a start configuration. We present a computationally efficient motion planner to compute this objective function for a given robotic design, and we use an asymptotically optimal simulated annealing optimizer to compute an optimized design. We applied our new method to optimize the design of a bimanual dexterous sheaths robot for performing procedures on cancerous polyps in colon anatomies, achieving a 78% higher RVDSA on average than optimizing for 3D voxel coverage alone.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a design optimization method for continuum robots that jointly considers dexterity and anatomy, using a novel Reachable Volumetric Dexterous Solid Angle (RVDSA) metric and a simulated annealing optimizer, validated on a bimanual dexterous sheath robot for colon polyp procedures.
AI.motivation: Continuum robots for complex medical procedures require careful geometric design parameter selection, and the robot must exhibit high dexterity within its specific anatomical environment, necessitating a design optimization approach that accounts for both dexterity and anatomy.
AI.method: The authors propose the Reachable Volumetric Dexterous Solid Angle (RVDSA) metric as the objective, which quantifies the end effector's ability to reach points in a goal volume from different directions via collision-free paths from a start configuration. A computationally efficient motion planner computes this objective for a given design, and an asymptotically optimal simulated annealing optimizer determines the optimized design.
AI.result: Applied to optimizing a bimanual dexterous sheath robot for procedures on cancerous polyps in colon anatomies, the method achieved a 78% higher RVDSA on average compared to optimizing for 3D voxel coverage alone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed anatomy-aware design optimization via the RVDSA metric yields substantially improved dexterity for continuum medical robots relative to coverage-only optimization.

title: HCOE: Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings from Biomedical Language Models
comment: Accepted at IEEE BIBM 2026. 7 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables
summary: Biomedical language models (LMs) encode textual semantics but do not explicitly preserve medical code hierarchies. We present Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings (HCOE) for hierarchy-aware clinical concept representation. HCOE maps frozen BioBERT embeddings into a Poincare ball, combining parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive learning with coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. It uses International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes organized by Clinical Classifications Software (CCS) and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) medication hierarchies. Evaluations show that HCOE performs best on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On the MIMIC-IV dataset, HCOE also achieves the best performance on mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.

AI.tldr: HCOE learns hierarchy-aware clinical concept embeddings by mapping frozen BioBERT vectors into a Poincaré ball with ontology-guided contrastive learning and coarse-to-fine path aggregation, improving clinical relation prediction, hierarchy transfer, and downstream MIMIC-IV tasks.
AI.motivation: Biomedical language models capture textual semantics but do not explicitly preserve medical code hierarchies, limiting their ability to represent clinical concepts in a hierarchy-aware manner.
AI.method: HCOE maps frozen BioBERT embeddings into a Poincaré ball (hyperbolic space). It combines parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive learning with coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. It leverages ICD codes organized by CCS and ATC medication hierarchies.
AI.result: HCOE performs best on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On MIMIC-IV, it also achieves the best performance on mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.
AI.conclusion: Injecting ontology hierarchy into hyperbolic embeddings over frozen biomedical LMs yields superior clinical concept representation and consistent gains across relational and downstream clinical prediction tasks.

title: Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform
summary:
Insurance reserve estimation is a fundamental actuarial task supporting premium pricing, solvency assessment, financial reporting, capital planning, and risk management. Classical reserve methods based on Thiele's differential equation provide a rigorous and interpretable foundation for life insurance valuation, but repeated reserve calculations become computationally expensive in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation.
  This paper presents an Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform for term-life reserve modelling that combines a classical Thiele-equation solver with a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) enhanced by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses. The framework includes synthetic policy generation, risk-adjusted premium calculation, classical reserve trajectory generation, reserve-ratio dataset construction, configurable neural training, validation diagnostics, sensitivity and elasticity analysis, prototype optimization workflows, and interest-rate scenario testing. A key refinement is the use of premium ratio and the explicit separation of pricing-time and scenario-time interest-rate semantics.
  The final model uses seven features: elapsed time, issue age, pricing interest rate, scenario interest rate, premium ratio, sum assured, and mortality intensity. It predicts a standardized reserve ratio instead of raw reserve values, improving numerical stability across policies with different sums assured. The model achieved an R2 of 0.9887, MAE of 785.48, and RMSE of 1212.76 on the test set. On 200 policies, PINN/KINN inference was approximately 119.53 times faster than the classical solver. Results show strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance, while highlighting remaining limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.

AI.tldr: An Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform is developed that couples a classical Thiele-equation reserve solver with a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) augmented by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses, achieving R2 = 0.9887 and ~119.5x speedup over the classical solver.
AI.motivation: Classical reserve methods based on Thiele's differential equation are rigorous and interpretable for life insurance valuation, but repeated reserve computation becomes computationally expensive in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation.
AI.method: The platform integrates a Thiele-equation solver with a PINN enhanced by KINN losses, and includes synthetic policy generation, risk-adjusted premium calculation, classical reserve trajectory generation, reserve-ratio dataset construction, configurable neural training, validation diagnostics, sensitivity/elasticity analysis, prototype optimization, and interest-rate scenario testing. The model uses seven features (elapsed time, issue age, pricing interest rate, scenario interest rate, premium ratio, sum assured, mortality intensity) and predicts a standardized reserve ratio rather than raw reserves; premium ratio and separate pricing-time vs. scenario-time interest-rate semantics are key refinements.
AI.result: Test-set performance: R2 = 0.9887, MAE = 785.48, RMSE = 1212.76. On 200 policies, PINN/KINN inference was ~119.53 times faster than the classical solver. Strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance were observed, with remaining limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.conclusion: The PINN/KINN-based platform delivers accurate, physics-consistent, and substantially faster term-life reserve estimation while preserving classical interpretability, though monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization remain open challenges.

title: NavGen: Visual Generative Models as a Scalable Data Engine for Embodied 3D Navigation
summary: General-purpose robot models increasingly rely on large and diverse datasets. For embodied 3D navigation, however, existing data sources face a fundamental trade-off: simulated data can be generated at scale but often suffer from the visual sim-to-real gap, whereas real-world flight data provide realistic observations but are costly to collect. This paper studies another direction: the use of high-fidelity visual generative models as scalable data engines for embodied 3D navigation. We introduce NavGen, a text-to-video data generation pipeline that produces diverse vision-language navigation (VLN) episodes across indoor and outdoor scenes. We also propose a style-diversification method that scales up long-tail data that are difficult and costly to collect. The resulting dataset contains approximately 400K navigation episodes. We evaluate our dataset against existing UAV navigation datasets across multiple metrics, and find that the model trained on our data generally improves with scale, outperforming those trained on existing datasets. To validate real-world transferability, we deploy the trained model in world-action-model paradigm to real-world flying experiments. The final model achieves a 75\% success rate across different navigation tasks and environments.

AI.tldr: NavGen is a text-to-video data generation pipeline that uses high-fidelity visual generative models to produce large-scale vision-language navigation episodes, yielding ~400K episodes and enabling a model with 75% real-world success rate.
AI.motivation: Embodied 3D navigation data faces a trade-off: simulated data scales but suffers a visual sim-to-real gap, while real-world flight data is realistic but costly. This motivates using high-fidelity visual generative models as scalable data engines.
AI.method: The authors introduce NavGen, a text-to-video data generation pipeline producing diverse VLN episodes across indoor and outdoor scenes, plus a style-diversification method to scale up long-tail, hard-to-collect data.
AI.result: The dataset contains ~400K navigation episodes. Evaluated against existing UAV navigation datasets on multiple metrics, models trained on this data generally improve with scale and outperform those trained on existing datasets. Real-world flying experiments under a world-action-model paradigm achieve a 75% success rate across different tasks and environments.
AI.conclusion: High-fidelity visual generative models can serve as effective, scalable data engines for embodied 3D navigation, delivering strong real-world transferability.

title: Does Thinking Help Fairness? Reasoning Tokens Resolve Some Biases but Create More
comment: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Thinking in reasoning language models (RLMs) has been subject to debate on whether it resolves or amplifies bias. Prior works have shown competing conclusions in both directions. Using a within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit), we show that thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it both resolves counterfactual flips produced by the non-thinking baseline and creates new flips at near-saturating model confidence. In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, the created flips outnumber the resolved flips by roughly 5 times. To explain the effect, we treat the thinking trace itself as a measurable site of fairness change and study it through two dynamic instruments: 1) We propose Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and observe that bias propagates and amplifies with thinking. 2) We also formulate the Bias Transition Matrix (BTM) to show how predictions of counterfactual pairs change from non-thinking to thinking, and find that the asymmetric dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition.

AI.tldr: Thinking in reasoning language models has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it resolves some counterfactual flips while creating roughly 5x more, across all nine (model, dataset) combinations studied.
AI.motivation: Prior work offers competing conclusions on whether reasoning/thinking resolves or amplifies bias. This paper aims to settle the debate with a controlled within-model comparison and to explain the mechanism behind the effect.
AI.method: A within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit). Two dynamic instruments are proposed: Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and Bias Transition Matrix (BTM) to capture how counterfactual pair predictions change from non-thinking to thinking.
AI.result: In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, created flips outnumber resolved flips by roughly 5x. Created flips occur at near-saturating model confidence. Bias propagates and amplifies with thinking depth (CDPG), and the asymmetric dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition (BTM).
AI.conclusion: Thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness, both resolving and creating counterfactual flips, with creation dominating. The effect is traceable to the joint transition dynamics of counterfactual pairs, positioning the thinking trace as a measurable site of fairness change.

title: ConsultMind:Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning
summary: Diagnostic consultation is an online sequential decision-making process in which clinicians gather evidence through patient interaction until a diagnosis is sufficiently supported. Automating this process requires adaptive inquiry and interpretable decisions. Bayesian networks offer a natural foundation by updating diagnostic posteriors as evidence accumulates, but their use in open-ended consultation raises two challenges: linking diagnostic hypotheses to potential inquiries and translating evolving posteriors into consultation decisions. We introduce AutoDisym, an automated pipeline that integrates diagnostic knowledge with heterogeneous diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives to construct a Disorder--Symptom Bayesian Network (DSBN). Building on the DSBN, we propose ConsultMind, an uncertainty-aware framework that updates disorder posteriors after each response and uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis. We evaluate both methods across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets. The results show that AutoDisym can automatically construct high-quality DSBNs and that ConsultMind consistently improves diagnostic performance and explanation soundness. For example, AutoDisym achieves macro-averaged F1 scores of 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations using GPT-5.6-Sol. ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points, respectively. Physician evaluation further shows that ConsultMind improves the quality of ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across LLMs of different scales. This work offers a promising approach to automatic diagnostic consultation.

AI.tldr: AutoDisym builds a Disorder–Symptom Bayesian Network from diagnoses and clinical narratives; ConsultMind uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis, improving diagnostic accuracy and explanation quality across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and public datasets.
AI.motivation: Automating diagnostic consultation requires adaptive inquiry and interpretable decisions. Bayesian networks naturally update diagnostic posteriors as evidence accumulates, but applying them to open-ended consultation faces two challenges: linking diagnostic hypotheses to potential inquiries, and translating evolving posteriors into consultation decisions.
AI.method: AutoDisym: an automated pipeline integrating diagnostic knowledge with heterogeneous diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives to construct a Disorder–Symptom Bayesian Network (DSBN). ConsultMind: an uncertainty-aware framework built on DSBN that updates disorder posteriors after each response and uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis.
AI.result: Evaluated across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets. AutoDisym constructs high-quality DSBNs, achieving macro-averaged F1 of 81.37 (canonical symptoms) and 72.19 (manifestations) with GPT-5.6-Sol. ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points. Physician evaluation shows improved ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across LLMs of different scales.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a promising approach to automatic diagnostic consultation, combining automated Bayesian network construction with uncertainty-guided inquiry and diagnosis.

title: HasMem: Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary: Text-based memory and context compression support reuse of past interactions. Resizing continuous memory changes the input to a frozen LLM, coupling capacity allocation with readout. We propose Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem). Frozen hard-prompt embeddings provide a verifiable initial state. A controller adjusts memory widths, a Writer re-encodes resized entries, and Reader and Global provide readout adaptation and cross-turn state. On all $535$ questions in a reconstruction probe derived from the Multi-Session Chat (MSC) development split, the main configuration achieves lexical F1 of $95.3$ ($+4.4$ percentage points) at $93.6\%$ of the hard reference's framed memory positions. With approximately matched per-question target body budgets, six configurations at mean per-entry retention around $0.83$--$0.91$ exceed rule-based re-encoding by $8.0$--$23.6$ exact-match (EM) percentage points. With fixed model parameters and rule target width ratio $0.75$, Global's EM gain passes a user-level exact paired test with Bonferroni correction over eight comparisons. On all $500$ LongMemEval-S questions, local lexical F1 rises from the hard reference's $3.4$ to $8.9$, and answer negative log-likelihood (NLL) falls from $12.257$ to $5.274$. F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations.

AI.tldr: HasMem decouples memory capacity allocation from readout in frozen LLMs by pairing a resizable, re-encoded continuous memory with Reader and Global readout-adaptation modules. It improves lexical F1 and answer NLL over hard-prompt references on MSC and LongMemEval-S, though exact match declines.
AI.motivation: Text-based memory and context compression allow past interactions to be reused, but resizing continuous memory alters the input to a frozen LLM, coupling capacity allocation with readout and making the memory difficult to verify or adapt.
AI.method: Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem): frozen hard-prompt embeddings give a verifiable initial state; a controller adjusts memory widths, a Writer re-encodes resized entries, and Reader and Global modules provide readout adaptation and cross-turn state.
AI.result: On all 535 MSC-derived reconstruction-probe questions, the main configuration reaches lexical F1 95.3 (+4.4 points) at 93.6% of the hard reference's framed memory positions. At roughly matched per-question target body budgets, six configurations with mean per-entry retention 0.83-0.91 exceed rule-based re-encoding by 8.0-23.6 EM points. With fixed parameters and rule target width ratio 0.75, Global's EM gain passes a user-level exact paired test with Bonferroni correction over eight comparisons. On all 500 LongMemEval-S questions, local lexical F1 rises from 3.4 to 8.9 and answer NLL falls from 12.257 to 5.274. F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations.
AI.conclusion: HasMem decouples capacity allocation from readout through a verifiable hard-origin initial state plus writer and readout-adaptation modules, yielding substantial lexical-F1 and NLL improvements at comparable memory budgets, but with an F1-EM trade-off that reduces exact match.

title: Evaluation Is All You Need for Multi-Modal Autonomous Driving
summary: Multi-modal planning is promising for autonomous driving by representing multiple plausible behaviors in ambiguous and long-tail scenarios. Existing methods mainly focus on improving trajectory multi-modality, enhancing trajectory representations, or reshaping the candidate distribution. Nevertheless, we identify a pronounced generation-evaluation asymmetry in multi-modal planning: despite strong oracle performance, existing planners often fail to reliably select the best available candidate, leaving substantial planning potential unrealized. To address this challenge, we propose iDriveVLA, a multi-modal planning framework that improves the candidate trajectory space while enabling more reliable and context-aware trajectory evaluation. Specifically, iDriveVLA introduces a unified trajectory evaluator comprising a Safety-aware Scorer for quality and risk estimation, together with a VLM-guided Modulator for scene-adaptive criterion weighting. We further develop an oracle-aligned progressive training strategy consisting of candidate imitation pretraining, candidate space refinement, and semantic ranking alignment. On the public NAVSIM v1 leaderboard, iDriveVLA achieves a new state-of-the-art performance of 94.95 PDMS, surpassing the human-expert reference.

AI.tldr: iDriveVLA is a multi-modal planning framework for autonomous driving that identifies and addresses a generation-evaluation asymmetry, achieving 94.95 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and surpassing human-expert reference.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal planners focus on improving trajectory multi-modality, representations, or candidate distribution, yet exhibit a pronounced generation-evaluation asymmetry: strong oracle performance but unreliable selection of the best available candidate, leaving substantial planning potential unrealized.
AI.method: iDriveVLA improves the candidate trajectory space while enabling reliable, context-aware trajectory evaluation. It introduces a unified trajectory evaluator with a Safety-aware Scorer for quality and risk estimation and a VLM-guided Modulator for scene-adaptive criterion weighting, plus an oracle-aligned progressive training strategy: candidate imitation pretraining, candidate space refinement, and semantic ranking alignment.
AI.result: On the public NAVSIM v1 leaderboard, iDriveVLA achieves 94.95 PDMS, a new state-of-the-art, surpassing the human-expert reference.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the generation-evaluation asymmetry through improved candidate space and reliable context-aware evaluation yields state-of-the-art multi-modal planning performance exceeding human-expert level.

title: Evaluating Real-Time Voice Agents: From Component Quality to Grounded Outcomes
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Corpus metadata, SHA-256 provenance hashes, and TRG reporting-standard tooling available at https://github.com/shivamnegi92/voice-agent-eval-corpus
summary: Real-time voice agents have moved from research prototypes to production deployments, yet the literature describing them is fragmented across three communities that rarely cite one another: speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, and agentic evaluation. Architecture papers report latency, turn-taking papers report prediction accuracy, and agentic benchmarks report task success, so no single number describes whether a deployed agent is actually good. We address that gap with three evidence-based claims, each traceable to a corpus of 38 primary sources organised into an application-centric taxonomy of six categories. First, architecture choice is a deployment constraint rather than a settled verdict: a 2026 enterprise tutorial reports that no fully self-hostable end-to-end system yet meets production constraints, while a chunked cascade independently reaches state-of-the-art duplex behaviour, showing duplex behaviour is separable from duplex architecture. Second, evaluation has shifted decisively from component quality toward grounded outcomes, with recent benchmarks verifying backend state rather than trusting what the agent claims to have done. Third, the dyadic assumption in most models and benchmarks is breaking down: multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning benchmarks show that deciding when not to speak, and reasoning about who may be told what, are first-class capabilities two-participant framings cannot measure. For each source we state the problem it targets, its mechanism, and its reported evidence, alongside the search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv identifier in circulation. We propose TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded), a reporting standard characterising an agent by timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome together, with a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys the fragmented real-time voice-agent literature (speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, agentic evaluation) across 38 primary sources in a six-category taxonomy, advances three evidence-based claims about architecture, evaluation, and dyadic assumptions, and proposes TRG, a reporting standard based on timing, recovery, and state-verified outcomes with an optional multiparty axis.
AI.motivation: Real-time voice agents are now in production, but the literature describing them is split across three largely non-citing communities: speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, and agentic evaluation. Each reports a different metric (latency, prediction accuracy, task success), so no single number captures whether a deployed agent is actually good. The paper addresses this evaluation fragmentation.
AI.method: A structured, evidence-based survey: 38 primary sources organised into an application-centric taxonomy of six categories, with a documented search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv identifier in circulation. For each source, the problem targeted, mechanism, and reported evidence are stated. Three claims are derived: (1) architecture choice is a deployment constraint, not a settled verdict; (2) evaluation has shifted from component quality to grounded, state-verified outcomes; (3) dyadic assumptions are breaking down. The proposed TRG reporting standard characterises an agent along timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome, with a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployment.
AI.result: A 2026 enterprise tutorial reports no fully self-hostable end-to-end system yet meets production constraints, while a chunked cascade independently reaches state-of-the-art duplex behaviour, showing duplex behaviour is separable from duplex architecture. Recent benchmarks verify backend state rather than trusting agent self-reports. Multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning benchmarks show that deciding when not to speak, and reasoning about who may be told what, are first-class capabilities that two-participant framings cannot measure. The verification step exposed a misattributed arXiv identifier.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that no single existing metric adequately characterises a deployed voice agent, and that reporting should be multi-axis. TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded) is proposed as a reporting standard combining timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome, plus a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployments, to unify evaluation across the three fragmented communities.

title: A Benchmark and Diagnostic Study of Epistemic Admission in Shared Agent Memory
summary: Evaluating claim admission in shared agent memory is challenging because repeated claims may be mistaken for independent evidence. An agent may copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, while admitting a false claim exposes subsequent agents to it. To study this problem, we introduce the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB), which evaluates whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory.CPB-Static constructs a frozen test split from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions. CPB-Live runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, and tracks source lineage defined by each scenario. A separate consumer answers from the store alone. We evaluate eight admission policies across four agent families. Our results show that policies which deduplicate sources reject many true claims alongside false ones, whereas policies preserving answer coverage admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type reduces false adoption to 0.06--0.09, compared with 0.22--0.47 for other answering policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97--0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative. These findings reveal the limitations of admission policies without access to source lineage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB) to evaluate claim admission in shared agent memory, showing that policies without source lineage cannot reliably reject false claims, while gating on declared source type substantially reduces false adoption.
AI.motivation: Repeated claims in shared agent memory may be mistaken for independent evidence: an agent can copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, and admitting a false claim exposes all subsequent agents to it. This creates a need to determine whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory.
AI.method: CPB comprises two components: CPB-Static, a frozen test split built from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions; and CPB-Live, which runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, tracks source lineage per scenario, and uses a separate consumer that answers from the store alone. Eight admission policies are evaluated across four agent families.
AI.result: Source-deduplicating policies reject many true claims alongside false ones, while answer-coverage-preserving policies admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type lowers false adoption to 0.06–0.09 versus 0.22–0.47 for other answering policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97–0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative.
AI.conclusion: Admission policies lacking access to source lineage have fundamental limitations and cannot reliably distinguish repeated claims from independent evidence. Only source-type gating approaches the reliability needed, underscoring that source lineage is essential for robust memory admission.

title: PTC-Decoder: Towards Intelligent SLMs on Offline Resource-Constrained Edge Devices
summary: Deploying small language models (SLMs) on offline, resource-constrained edge devices such as remote sensing satellites presents a fundamental challenge: their limited reasoning capacity hinders reliable execution of multi-step agent tasks requiring complex tool orchestration. Existing plan-solve paradigms rely on prompt-based enforcement, which our experiments show SLMs almost entirely disregard: weak models fail to invoke the plan. We propose PTC-Decoder (Plan-Tool Constrained Decoder), a training-free, plug-and-play decoder framework that combines (1) a Plan-to-Act paradigm, which elevates planning to an atomic tool and forces its invocation at the first inference step, and (2) TC-Decoder, a deterministic finite automaton that imposes token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation, thereby retaining SLM reasoning capability. Evaluated on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs, PTC-Decoder yields a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01), 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and other datasets. An ablation study that removes TC-Decoder causes substantial performance degradation across all quality metrics without reducing computational cost, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver. PTC-Decoder thus offers a lightweight yet effective solution for improving step-level reliability, with final-answer accuracy remaining an open challenge. In essence, we enforce plan adherence by constraining the permissible output vocabulary during inference, without requiring retraining.

AI.tldr: PTC-Decoder is a training-free, plug-and-play decoder framework that improves plan adherence and tool orchestration in small language models by constraining the output vocabulary during inference, without retraining.
AI.motivation: Deploying SLMs on offline, resource-constrained edge devices (e.g., remote sensing satellites) is limited by their weak reasoning capacity, which hinders reliable execution of multi-step agent tasks requiring complex tool orchestration. Existing plan-solve paradigms rely on prompt-based enforcement, which the authors show SLMs almost entirely disregard: weak models fail to invoke the plan.
AI.method: PTC-Decoder combines two components: (1) a Plan-to-Act paradigm that elevates planning to an atomic tool and forces its invocation at the first inference step, and (2) TC-Decoder, a deterministic finite automaton that imposes token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation, thereby retaining SLM reasoning capability. The framework is training-free and plug-and-play.
AI.result: Evaluated on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs, PTC-Decoder achieves a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01, 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and other datasets. An ablation removing TC-Decoder causes substantial degradation across all quality metrics without reducing computational cost, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver.
AI.conclusion: PTC-Decoder offers a lightweight yet effective solution for improving step-level reliability in SLMs, though final-answer accuracy remains an open challenge. The approach enforces plan adherence by constraining the permissible output vocabulary during inference, without requiring retraining.

title: Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis
summary: Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query's safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other's blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

AI.tldr: The paper interprets dLLM safety alignment as an energy landscape with a barrier separating safe and harmful regions, unifying jailbreak attacks into two strategies and deriving three training-free complementary detection signals validated across four dLLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed.
AI.method: The authors interpret safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape, where aligned models route harmful queries to safe outputs via an energy barrier. Jailbreak attacks are reduced to two strategies: obscuring the query's safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the barrier. Leveraging the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, they derive three training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio reading initial safety disposition from the logit distribution pre-generation, and two trajectory-velocity signals tracking kinetic energy in complementary logit-space subspaces.
AI.result: Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms the complementarity of the three signals. In stress tests, every configuration evading detection also fails to produce harmful content.
AI.conclusion: The three signals cover each other's blind spots in the energy budget by construction, since an attack must either reveal intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in a monitored subspace. The finding that evasion coincides with failure to produce harmful content suggests detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

title: SkillEvoReg: Regularizing Agent Skill Evolution Against Overfitting
summary: Language-model agents increasingly improve by converting execution experience into reusable external skills. Yet repeated skill updates form a learning process of their own: locally useful edits can accumulate into redundant or task-specific instructions, while new updates can disrupt behavior that previously worked. We study this problem as skill-evolution overfitting and introduce SkillEvoReg, a general regularization framework for skill evolution inspired by anti-overfitting techniques in neural-network training. SkillEvoReg combines training-time skill dropout, which perturbs update generation, and complexity-aware local regularization, which controls unnecessary structural growth, with causal counterexample validation (CCV), which provides targeted behavioral validation of candidate-specific regressions. We instantiate the framework across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while retaining each system's native skill evolver and task evaluator. Across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, SkillEvoReg consistently controls skill-state growth while preserving competitive downstream capability, improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes, and identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal. These results suggest that explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "skill-evolution overfitting" in language-model agents that convert execution experience into reusable external skills, and proposes SkillEvoReg, a regularization framework that mitigates it.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents improve by converting execution experience into reusable external skills, but repeated skill updates form a learning process of their own. Locally useful edits can accumulate into redundant or task-specific instructions, and new updates can disrupt previously working behavior. The authors frame this as skill-evolution overfitting.
AI.method: SkillEvoReg is a general regularization framework for skill evolution, inspired by anti-overfitting techniques in neural-network training. It combines training-time skill dropout (perturbing update generation), complexity-aware local regularization (controlling unnecessary structural growth), and causal counterexample validation (CCV) for targeted behavioral validation of candidate-specific regressions. It is instantiated across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while retaining each system's native skill evolver and task evaluator.
AI.result: Across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, SkillEvoReg consistently controls skill-state growth while preserving competitive downstream capability, improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes, and identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal.
AI.conclusion: Explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters. SkillEvoReg addresses skill-evolution overfitting by controlling growth, preserving capability, and surfacing behavioral regressions.

title: TISD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Trajectory Intervention
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense teacher targets, but evaluates them only along student-sampled rollouts. When the privileged teacher favors an alternative action at a visited prefix, OPSD can provide a target for the branch decision but cannot supervise the successor contexts induced by that action unless the student samples it. This creates a training-time data-collection bottleneck and suggests a different role for teacher-student disagreement: proposing a trajectory branch rather than identifying a sufficient local repair. Our diagnostic framework using controlled token interventions reveals that a teacher-preferred token at peak disagreement can improve student continuation success, while its local corrective value is limited. Motivated by this finding, we introduce a simple branch-regenerate-distill algorithm, Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD). TISD forces a teacher-selected branch action, returns suffix generation to the student, and distills the full trajectory under the privileged-context-conditioned teacher. Across the coding models, TISD improves average Avg@4 over SDPO by 1.2 percentage points. Across the science domains, it improves average Avg@128 by 0.8 points under an equal-step budget and by 0.3 points under an equal-time budget. These results support teacher-guided branching as a way to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation.

AI.tldr: OPSD supervises teacher targets only along student-sampled rollouts, bottlenecking data collection. TISD instead forces a teacher-selected branch action, lets the student regenerate the suffix, and distills the full trajectory under a privileged-context teacher, improving coding and science benchmarks over SDPO.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense teacher targets but evaluates them only along student-sampled rollouts. When the privileged teacher prefers an alternative action at a visited prefix, OPSD can supervise the branch decision but cannot supervise the successor contexts induced by that action unless the student samples it. This creates a training-time data-collection bottleneck and motivates reinterpreting teacher-student disagreement: as a proposal of a trajectory branch rather than a sufficient local repair.
AI.method: A diagnostic framework using controlled token interventions shows that a teacher-preferred token at peak disagreement can improve student continuation success, while its local corrective value is limited. Motivated by this, the authors propose Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD), a simple branch-regenerate-distill algorithm: it forces a teacher-selected branch action, returns suffix generation to the student, and distills the full trajectory under the privileged-context-conditioned teacher.
AI.result: Across coding models, TISD improves average Avg@4 over SDPO by 1.2 percentage points. Across science domains, it improves average Avg@128 by 0.8 points under an equal-step budget and by 0.3 points under an equal-time budget.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-guided branching is an effective way to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation, overcoming the rollout-coverage bottleneck of standard OPSD.

title: EXAONE Demand 1.0: A Time Series Foundation Model for Demand Forecasting
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on series from diverse domains, where demand series make up only a small fraction. Demand data has properties that such corpora rarely contain: Short histories, frequent zeros, censoring by stock-outs, and exogenous events that the series does not record. To this end, we propose EXAONE Demand, built on 1) a demand-specific corpus and 2) a demand-aware adapter. For the corpus, we assemble 11.3M series and 48.4B observations from 73 sources, and a synthetic generator supplies the behaviour that open demand data under-represents. For the adapter, we attach low-rank branches to a frozen general-domain backbone, one for each of the four demand classes (smooth, intermittent, erratic, and lumpy), and a router that reads eight scale-free statistics of the input series decides how much each branch contributes. We build EXAONE Demand in two versions, one trained on real-world and synthetic demand together and one trained on the synthetic corpus alone. On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 TSFMs, and real-world demand adds a gain over synthetic data alone.

AI.tldr: EXAONE Demand is a time series foundation model specialized for demand forecasting, trained on a large demand-specific corpus (real + synthetic) and equipped with a demand-aware low-rank adapter with class-specific branches and a router over scale-free statistics, outperforming 36 TSFMs on 22 held-out datasets.
AI.motivation: General time series foundation models are pretrained on diverse domains where demand series are a small fraction, yet demand data has distinctive properties—short histories, frequent zeros, stock-out censoring, and unrecorded exogenous events—that such corpora rarely contain, limiting their effectiveness for demand forecasting.
AI.method: They build a demand-specific corpus of 11.3M series and 48.4B observations from 73 sources, supplemented by a synthetic generator that supplies under-represented demand behaviors. On a frozen general-domain backbone they attach a demand-aware adapter: low-rank branches, one per demand class (smooth, intermittent, erratic, lumpy), plus a router that reads eight scale-free statistics of the input series to weight each branch's contribution. Two versions are trained: one on real-world and synthetic demand together, one on synthetic alone.
AI.result: On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 TSFMs, and real-world demand data provides an additional gain over synthetic data alone.
AI.conclusion: Combining a demand-specific corpus with a demand-aware adapter yields a specialized TSFM that surpasses general TSFMs for demand forecasting, with real demand data complementing synthetic data.

title: From Tapping to Hopping: Augmenting Mobile GUI Agents with App-Native Deeplinks
summary: Mobile GUI agents complete tasks using GUI actions like taps and swipes. These actions are broadly applicable across applications, but reaching a navigation interface. A single deeplink call can replace a sequence of screen-by-screen GUI actions. We therefore introduce hybrid interaction, using deeplinks for direct navigation and GUI actions for other on-screen operations and fallback. To enable this, we discover candidate deeplinks through static analysis, validate them on real devices, and describe their observed landing screens. This process creates a verified and grounded deeplink catalog that pairs each working deeplink with a description of its landing screen. Using this catalog, we introduce GUI-Hopper, a improves task success in commercial applications on real devices, further demonstrating the benefits of hybrid interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "hybrid interaction" for mobile GUI agents, combining deeplink-based direct navigation with GUI actions, and builds a verified deeplink catalog plus the GUI-Hopper agent.
AI.motivation: GUI actions like taps and swipes are broadly applicable across apps but inefficient for reaching a navigation interface, where a single deeplink call can replace a long sequence of screen-by-screen GUI actions.
AI.method: Hybrid interaction using deeplinks for direct navigation and GUI actions for other on-screen operations and fallback. Candidate deeplinks are discovered through static analysis, validated on real devices, and their landing screens described, yielding a verified and grounded deeplink catalog. Based on this catalog, GUI-Hopper is introduced.
AI.result: GUI-Hopper improves task success in commercial applications on real devices, further demonstrating the benefits of hybrid interaction.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid interaction, enabled by a verified and grounded deeplink catalog, improves task success for mobile GUI agents in commercial applications on real devices.

title: Training Graph Foundation Models on The Web Graph
summary: We introduce Acacia, a graph foundation model, trained on the web graph. Acacia (i) supports arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics without additional training, (ii) supports a wide range of tasks, including node classification, link prediction, node clustering, and graph generation, without additional training, (iii) has in-context learning capabilities, and (iv) does not rely on pretrained LLMs. In particular, existing graph foundation models often require training additional classification heads or feature projectors to accommodate new graphs or new labels, whereas Acacia does not. Moreover, existing graph foundation models often gain their capabilities by being stitched together with pretrained LLMs, whereas Acacia is trained from scratch using only the Common Crawl web graph. This is also an important result because it provides evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch like LLMs.

AI.tldr: Acacia is a graph foundation model trained on the web graph that supports arbitrary feature dimensionalities, a wide range of tasks, and in-context learning without additional training or reliance on pretrained LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing graph foundation models often require training additional classification heads or feature projectors to accommodate new graphs or labels, and frequently gain their capabilities by being stitched together with pretrained LLMs rather than being genuinely graph-native.
AI.method: Acacia is trained from scratch using only the Common Crawl web graph, without pretrained LLMs, and is designed to support arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics, multiple tasks (node classification, link prediction, node clustering, graph generation), and in-context learning without additional training.
AI.result: Acacia achieves its design goals: it avoids the need for additional classification heads or feature projectors, supports a broad task range without extra training, and acquires emergent capabilities from scratch.
AI.conclusion: The work provides evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch like LLMs, demonstrating that graph foundation models need not depend on pretrained LLMs.

title: JevSoup: System-One Routing for Training-Free LoRA Composition
summary: Building adaptable AI systems requires effective coordination of specialized capabilities across diverse tasks. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables modular expertise, but existing routing approaches may require auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding. We propose JevSoup, a training-free framework separating System One expert routing from System Two execution. Using only the input and expert descriptions, Jev selects two experts through structured probabilities. JevSoup retains the leading expert's update, projects the second onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space, and combines them with equal weights. Across 14 PorTAL tasks and three Qwen3 scales, JepSoup achieves absolute gains of up to 1.19\% in task-macro and 1.21\% in sample-micro accuracy over the strongest evaluated external baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/Leowang980/JevSoup.

AI.tldr: JevSoup is a training-free framework for routing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) experts, separating expert routing (System One) from execution (System Two). Selecting two experts via structured probabilities, it retains the top expert's update and projects the second onto the orthogonal complement of the first's row space, combining them with equal weights. It achieves up to 1.19% task-macro and 1.21% sample-micro accuracy gains on 14 PorTAL tasks across three Qwen3 scales.
AI.motivation: Building adaptable AI systems requires effective coordination of specialized capabilities across diverse tasks. LoRA enables modular expertise, but existing routing approaches may require auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding, limiting their practicality.
AI.method: JevSoup is a training-free framework that separates System One expert routing from System Two execution. Using only the input and expert descriptions, it selects two experts through structured probabilities. It retains the leading expert's update, projects the second onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space, and combines them with equal weights.
