AI.result: Across 14 PorTAL tasks and three Qwen3 scales, JevSoup achieves absolute gains of up to 1.19% in task-macro and 1.21% in sample-micro accuracy over the strongest evaluated external baselines.
AI.conclusion: JevSoup provides an effective, training-free approach to coordinating LoRA experts, improving accuracy over strong baselines without auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding.

title: Self-Play Search Distillation for Large Language Model Reasoning
summary: Improving reasoning abilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) requires high-quality data that exposes difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and their consequences. Data scarcity is driven by the low quality of synthetic data and the cost of human labeling. We introduce Self-Play Search Distillation (SPSD), a framework for generating superhuman synthetic data via self-play of MuZero-like networks trained on board games. SPSD uses executable environments to turn search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, the expert identifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates. By converting the self-play search records into superhuman chains-of-thought, we train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision. Although trained only on self-play search records, SPSD transfers to unseen mathematics. On Qwen3-4B-Base, it raises the mean over six mathematics benchmarks from 24.1 to 36.6 while increasing the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%. SPSD offers an annotation-efficient way to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM performance in reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: SPSD generates superhuman synthetic reasoning data via self-play of MuZero-like networks on board games, converting search records into chains-of-thought that transfer to unseen mathematics.
AI.motivation: Improving LLM reasoning requires high-quality data exposing difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and their consequences. Such data is scarce due to the low quality of synthetic data and the high cost of human labeling.
AI.method: SPSD leverages executable board-game environments to turn search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, an expert network identifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates. These self-play search records are converted into superhuman chains-of-thought, used to train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision.
AI.result: Trained only on self-play search records, SPSD transfers to unseen mathematics. On Qwen3-4B-Base, it raises the mean over six mathematics benchmarks from 24.1 to 36.6, and increases the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%.
AI.conclusion: SPSD provides an annotation-efficient way to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM reasoning performance, demonstrating transfer from board-game self-play to mathematical reasoning.

title: MACBT: A Multi-Agent Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Decision Support System with Longitudinal Memory
summary: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based first-line treatment for depression, yet its scale is constrained by the time clinicians spend on pre-session preparation, post-session documentation, and longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking. We present a clinician-facing AI decision-support system that combines a multi-agent CBT framework (MACBT) with a CBT-specific longitudinal memory module (CD Memory). MACBT encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and treatment monitoring) into five collaborative agents. CD Memory tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions to generate pre-session pathology reports and intervention-priority recommendations. We construct a Chinese CBT dialogue corpus via dual-role large language model simulation and train a Qwen3-14B backbone with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Evaluation with GPT-4 judges shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The full memory-augmented system further improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.

AI.tldr: A clinician-facing AI decision-support system combining a multi-agent CBT framework (MACBT) with a CBT-specific longitudinal memory module (CD Memory) improves session quality and cross-session continuity in depression treatment.
AI.motivation: CBT is an evidence-based first-line treatment for depression, but its scalability is limited by the substantial clinician time required for pre-session preparation, post-session documentation, and longitudinal tracking of cognitive pathology.
AI.method: The system integrates MACBT, which encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, treatment monitoring) into five collaborative agents, with CD Memory, which tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions to generate pre-session pathology reports and intervention-priority recommendations. A Chinese CBT dialogue corpus was built via dual-role LLM simulation, and a Qwen3-14B backbone was trained with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization.
AI.result: GPT-4-judge evaluation shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The memory-augmented system improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent, memory-augmented AI system offers scalable clinician decision support for CBT, enhancing both single-session quality and longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking.

title: Financial Fragility in Societies of LLM Agents: Coordination Failures and Stabilizing Mechanisms
summary: Individually protective decisions can produce avoidable collective failures. As large language model (LLM) agents take on greater roles in financial decision-making, financial AI safety must therefore be considered not only at the level of individual agents, but also at the level of the systems they jointly create. We study this problem with FRAIL, a controlled experimental framework that places LLM agents in three dynamic financial environments---bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding---where agents' decisions reshape the financial conditions faced by others. Across seven leading LLMs, we find widespread collective fragility even when no agent is instructed to destabilize the system: 77\% of baseline bank-run episodes and 83\% of debt-rollover episodes end in failure. We then compare three interaction mechanisms based on compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions. All three improve aggregate outcomes, but no single mechanism performs best across all financial structures. Across mechanisms, successful stabilization shares a common temporal pattern: broad commitment forms early, before defensive behavior becomes self-reinforcing. Our findings show that individually capable agents do not automatically form safe financial systems, highlighting system-level evaluation and interaction design as central problems for financial AI safety. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FinFrail-CF26.

AI.tldr: LLM agents placed in dynamic financial environments (bank runs, debt rollover, crowdfunding) frequently produce collective failures despite no instruction to destabilize, and while three commitment-based interaction mechanisms improve outcomes, no single one dominates—early, broad commitment is the common stabilizing pattern.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents take larger roles in financial decision-making, safety must be assessed not only at the individual-agent level but at the level of the systems they jointly create, since individually protective decisions can cause avoidable collective failures. The paper aims to evaluate and address this system-level financial AI safety problem.
AI.method: The authors introduce FRAIL, a controlled experimental framework placing LLM agents in three dynamic financial environments—bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding—where each agent's decisions reshape others' financial conditions. They test seven leading LLMs and compare three interaction mechanisms: compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions.
AI.result: Collective fragility is widespread even absent instructions to destabilize: 77% of baseline bank-run episodes and 83% of debt-rollover episodes end in failure. All three interaction mechanisms improve aggregate outcomes, but none is best across all financial structures. Successful stabilization consistently shares a temporal pattern: broad commitment forms early, before defensive behavior becomes self-reinforcing.
AI.conclusion: Individually capable LLM agents do not automatically form safe financial systems, making system-level evaluation and interaction design central problems for financial AI safety.

title: LogicTree-RAG: Logic Tree-guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Long-form Patent Drafting
summary: Long-form technical text generation underpins knowledge-intensive workflows, yet remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to the need for globally consistent logical structuring and faithful technical reasoning beyond local coherence. Patent drafting is a canonical instance of this challenge, demanding holistic generation of a legally compliant and technically exhaustive document through sustained multi-expert collaboration. Existing approaches often focus on partial section generation or rely on manually crafted outlines, limiting scalable automation in realistic settings. In this work, we propose LogicTree-RAG, a logic tree-guided retrieval-augmented generation framework that induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone to organize and ground technical disclosures, without relying on expert-defined drafting priors. Each node in the logic tree represents a technical element and is constructed through evidence-guided recursive generation. A hybrid traversal mechanism then maps the logic tree into patent sections, enabling controllable and section-balanced generation. Extensive experiments show that LogicTree-RAG consistently improves content quality and language conformity over strong LLM-based baselines and achieves longer structured generation with high token efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of logic-centric generation for complex technical document drafting.

AI.tldr: LogicTree-RAG induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global backbone to ground long-form patent drafting via evidence-guided recursive node generation and hybrid traversal, improving content quality and language conformity over LLM baselines.
AI.motivation: Long-form technical text generation requires globally consistent logical structuring and faithful technical reasoning, not just local coherence. Patent drafting exemplifies this challenge, needing holistic, legally compliant, technically exhaustive documents. Existing methods only generate partial sections or rely on manually crafted outlines, limiting scalable automation.
AI.method: A logic tree-guided retrieval-augmented generation framework. It induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone to organize and ground technical disclosures without expert-defined drafting priors. Each node represents a technical element, built via evidence-guided recursive generation. A hybrid traversal mechanism maps the logic tree into patent sections for controllable, section-balanced generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show LogicTree-RAG consistently improves content quality and language conformity over strong LLM-based baselines, achieving longer structured generation with high token efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Logic-centric generation is effective for complex technical document drafting, enabling scalable, controllable automation of patent drafting.

title: FTB Graph: Determining and Validating First-token Broadcasters and Language-Identity Head Circuits in Multilingual Language Models
comment: 14 pages including supplementary material, 13 figures, 6 tables
summary: Large language models operating in multilingual contexts must resolve target response languages early in generation, yet the causal circuitry governing first-token language identity decisions remains poorly mapped. We present an end-to-end structural circuit analysis across six model architectures spanning four families: GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct. Using Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping, followed by exact activation patching verification with a 2,000-candidate-edge search ceiling, we extract directed acyclic graphs driving first-token language broadcasting. Across the standalone models, we observe deep or mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs, though the evidence is strongest for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M because GPT-2 and Pythia-1B leave few out-of-graph heads for comparison, while both Qwen2.5-1.5B variants invert the necessity check. Scaling from Pythia-1B to 2.8B expands node participation while maintaining a similar verified edge budget, producing sparser topology. The Qwen2.5-1.5B base and instruct circuits retain 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including the Layer 27 hub, indicating that first-token routing is largely established during pretraining and preserved by instruction tuning. Finally, EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas across most models, showing that linear gradient approximations can diverge from causal interventions in FP16 and motivating exact-patching verification for reliable circuit discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper performs end-to-end structural circuit analysis of first-token language-identity decisions across six multilingual LLMs (GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct), using EAP with FP16 active clamping plus exact activation patching. It maps directed acyclic graphs of first-token language broadcasting, characterizes scaling effects, shows base/instruct circuit stability, and demonstrates that EAP scores diverge from true causal patching deltas.
AI.motivation: LLMs in multilingual contexts must commit to a target response language early in generation, and the causal circuitry behind the first-token language-identity decision is poorly mapped. Existing work lacks an end-to-end structural account of which components causally drive this decision.
AI.method: Structural circuit analysis over six architectures from four families (GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct). Circuit discovery via Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping, then exact activation patching verification under a 2,000-candidate-edge search ceiling, extracting directed acyclic graphs for first-token language broadcasting.
AI.result: Deep or mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs appear across standalone models, with strongest evidence for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M (GPT-2 and Pythia-1B leave few out-of-graph heads; Qwen2.5-1.5B variants invert the necessity check). Scaling Pythia-1B to 2.8B expands node participation at similar verified edge budget, yielding sparser topology. Qwen2.5-1.5B base and instruct circuits share 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including the Layer 27 hub. EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas in most models.
AI.conclusion: First-token language routing is largely established during pretraining and preserved by instruction tuning, as evidenced by high base/instruct circuit overlap. Linear gradient approximations (EAP) can diverge from causal interventions under FP16, motivating exact-patching verification for reliable circuit discovery.

title: MoMHa: Multi-Objective Optimization of LLM Harnesses over Accuracy, Safety, and Tokens
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Most work on improving large language models treats accuracy as the sole objective. We argue that the harness, the Python code surrounding the model that constructs prompts, routes calls, and parses outputs, is a first-class design surface whose quality is inherently multi-objective: an accurate harness that refuses no unsafe request, or that consumes an order of magnitude more tokens, is not a good harness. We present Meta-Harness, a system that casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioural safety, and token cost) solved by an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. Our central finding is that a singlephase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa) outperforms every alternative, including a two-phase "accuracy then tokens" ablation, scalar-only feedback, and an accuracy-only baseline. We evaluate on seventeen domains: seven synthetic capability suites, seven real-world public benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, Spider, FEVER, MMLU-Pro, LawBench, NuminaMath), and three U-SafeBench-derived user-specific safety domains, using a 12-model fleet spanning four families. On the synthetic track MoMHa achieves a joint mean of 0.482 versus 0.198-0.422 for ten baselines, winning $7 / 10$ per-domain columns; on the real-world track it scores 0.461 versus 0.377 for the strongest baseline (DSPy), winning 5/7 columns, demonstrating that harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8 of 12 target models. MoMHa attains the highest measured behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench, 0.781) and uses 95 fewer tokens per example than the two-phase alternative. We will release all harness code, evaluation infrastructure, and crossmodel logs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Meta-Harness, which reframes "harness" design (the Python code constructing prompts, routing calls, and parsing outputs around an LLM) as a multi-objective search problem over accuracy, behavioral safety, and token cost. An agentic proposer with filesystem access to prior harnesses, traces, and scores (MoMHa) solves this via single-phase joint reward and beats two-phase, scalar-only, and accuracy-only alternatives across 17 domains.
AI.motivation: Prior work on improving LLMs treats accuracy as the sole objective and overlooks the harness code surrounding the model. The authors argue harness quality is inherently multi-objective: a harness that is accurate but refuses no unsafe request, or consumes an order of magnitude more tokens, is not good. Harness design is thus a first-class design surface deserving systematic optimization rather than hand-crafting.
AI.method: Meta-Harness casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioral safety, token cost), solved by an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. The central method is a single-phase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa), compared against a two-phase "accuracy then tokens" ablation, scalar-only feedback, and an accuracy-only baseline. Evaluation covers 17 domains (7 synthetic capability suites, 7 real-world public benchmarks, 3 U-SafeBench-derived user-specific safety domains) using a 12-model fleet across four families.
AI.result: On the synthetic track MoMHa achieves a joint mean of 0.482 versus 0.198-0.422 for ten baselines, winning 7/10 per-domain columns. On the real-world track it scores 0.461 versus 0.377 for the strongest baseline (DSPy), winning 5/7 columns, and transfers to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8 of 12 target models. MoMHa attains the highest measured behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench, 0.781) and uses 95 fewer tokens per example than the two-phase alternative.
AI.conclusion: Single-phase joint-reward search (MoMHa) outperforms every alternative, including two-phase, scalar-only, and accuracy-only approaches, demonstrating that multi-objective harness optimization with an agentic proposer yields superior accuracy, safety, and cost efficiency, and that learned harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks. All harness code, evaluation infrastructure, and cross-model logs will be released.

title: SciHorizon-eLab: An Agentic Protocol-to-Task Compiler for Scalable Benchmarking of Scientific Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied agents offer a promising route to automating scientific experimentation, yet their progress is constrained by the lack of reliable and systematic evaluation environments. Existing simulation-based laboratory benchmarks rely heavily on manual task engineering, making it challenging to systematically compile diverse scientific protocols into executable and verifiable embodied tasks at scale. To address this challenge, we introduce SciHorizon-eLab, an agentic protocol-to-task compiler that formulates scientific embodied task construction as a compilation problem. Given a natural-language protocol of scientific experiments, SciHorizon-eLab progressively compiles laboratory protocols into semantic-preserving embodied tasks through semantic grounding, executable task synthesis, and multi-stage simulation-based certification. The system generates semantically grounded environments, executable manipulation programs, and step-level success specifications, while enabling reproducible generation of expert demonstrations and execution traces. Using this pipeline, we further construct \BenchName, a ready-to-use benchmark comprising 300 certified tasks across diverse laboratory operations. It supports HIL task execution, reproducible expert-demonstration generation, and ordered step-level evaluation. Across representative tasks, the strongest policy attains an average success rate of only 49.7%, with further evaluations revealing pronounced weaknesses in human and embodied agent coordination. We publicly release the code, benchmark data, and evaluation toolkit at https://github.com/SciHorizon-elab/SciHorizon-elab.

AI.tldr: SciHorizon-eLab is an agentic protocol-to-task compiler that turns natural-language lab protocols into executables, verifiable embodied tasks, and a 300-task benchmark with step-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents could automate scientific experimentation, but progress is limited by the lack of reliable, systematic evaluation environments. Existing simulation-based lab benchmarks depend on manual task engineering, making it hard to compile diverse scientific protocols into executable and verifiable embodied tasks at scale.
AI.method: The authors formulate scientific embodied task construction as a compilation problem and introduce SciHorizon-eLab, an agentic protocol-to-task compiler. Given a natural-language protocol, it progressively compiles protocols into semantic-preserving embodied tasks via semantic grounding, executable task synthesis, and multi-stage simulation-based certification. It generates semantically grounded environments, executable manipulation programs, and step-level success specifications, supporting reproducible expert demonstrations and execution traces. Using this pipeline, they build a 300-task benchmark spanning diverse laboratory operations, supporting HIL execution, reproducible demonstration generation, and ordered step-level evaluation.
AI.result: On representative tasks, the strongest policy achieves only 49.7% average success rate. Further evaluations reveal pronounced weaknesses in human and embodied agent coordination.
AI.conclusion: SciHorizon-eLab provides a scalable, systematic way to compile scientific protocols into certified embodied tasks and introduces a ready-to-use benchmark with step-level evaluation. Code, benchmark data, and evaluation toolkit are publicly released.

title: Factorized axis convolutional gated recurrent unit with dynamic adaptive pooling for remaining useful life prediction of rolling bearings
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of rolling bearings from time-frequency representations (TFRs) of vibration signals. However, during degradation, characteristic structures in TFRs align predominantly along the frequency or time axis, making it challenging for conventional CNN isotropic kernels to capture directional structure. Furthermore, global average pooling (GAP) averages across axes, potentially obscuring the locations and concentrations of salient activations. This study introduces a factorized-axis convolutional gated recurrent unit (GRU) that employs multiscale anisotropic convolution and dual-axis convolution block attention module to enhance directional features and highlight salient time-frequency regions. Dynamic adaptive pooling (DAP) adaptively aggregates the time-frequency-axis information from the extracted feature maps, whereas a GRU captures temporal dynamics in the latent representations and Monte Carlo dropout enables predictive uncertainty estimation. Experiments on two public bearing datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing RUL prediction methods across operating conditions. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the factorized axis-wise design achieves lower mean errors than convolutional isotropic kernels. DAP yields clear improvements on one dataset while matching GAP on the other, highlighting the importance of anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive feature aggregation for TFR-based RUL prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a factorized-axis convolutional GRU network with multiscale anisotropic convolution, dual-axis CBAM attention, and dynamic adaptive pooling to improve remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of rolling bearings from time-frequency representations.
AI.motivation: Conventional CNNs use isotropic kernels that struggle to capture directionally aligned degradation structures in TFRs, and GAP averages across axes, obscuring salient activation locations and concentrations. This limits RUL prediction accuracy from time-frequency vibration representations.
AI.method: A factorized-axis convolutional GRU is introduced, combining multiscale anisotropic convolution and a dual-axis convolution block attention module to enhance directional features and highlight salient time-frequency regions. Dynamic adaptive pooling (DAP) aggregates time- and frequency-axis information from feature maps, a GRU captures temporal dynamics in latent representations, and Monte Carlo dropout provides predictive uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on two public bearing datasets show the model outperforms existing RUL prediction methods across operating conditions. Ablations show the factorized axis-wise design yields lower mean errors than isotropic kernels; DAP clearly improves one dataset while matching GAP on the other.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive feature aggregation are important for TFR-based RUL prediction, validating the proposed factorized-axis convolutional GRU design.

title: Same Text, Different Numbers: The Divergence of LLM-Based Measures
summary: Researchers increasingly use generative large language models (LLMs) to convert corporate text into empirical variables. We examine the extent to which LLM-based textual measures are invariant to model choice using thirteen measures, including sentiment, management clarity, uncertainty, answer specificity, and climate and political risk. Seven LLMs from different providers score earnings call transcripts of S&P 500 companies on these constructs. Cross-model rank correlations average only 0.52, and transcript-level differences common across providers account for only 34% of total score variation. Cross-model disagreement does not predict subsequent analyst or market disagreement, consistent with a substantial model-specific component rather than common ambiguity in the underlying disclosure. Model choice significantly affects downstream inference, with coefficient magnitudes, signs, and statistical significance varying substantially across models. Averaging across providers makes transcript rankings more stable for most constructs, but score levels remain sensitive to the models included in the ensemble. LLM-generated variables should therefore be treated as model-contingent measurements and validated across providers.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates the reliability of LLM-based textual measures by applying thirteen constructs across seven LLMs from different providers to S&P 500 earnings call transcripts, finding that measures are largely model-contingent rather than model-invariant.
AI.motivation: Researchers increasingly convert corporate text into empirical variables using generative LLMs, but the extent to which resulting measures are invariant to model choice—and thus comparable across studies—remains unknown. This paper tests whether LLM-based textual measures are stable across models and whether they support consistent downstream inference.
AI.method: Thirteen textual measures (including sentiment, management clarity, uncertainty, answer specificity, and climate and political risk) were constructed from S&P 500 earnings call transcripts scored by seven LLMs from different providers. The authors assess cross-model rank correlations, decompose score variation into transcript-level and provider/model-specific components, test whether cross-model disagreement predicts analyst or market disagreement, compare downstream regression inference across models, and evaluate ensembling across providers.
AI.result: Average cross-model rank correlations are only 0.52. Transcript-level differences common across providers explain just 34% of total score variation. Cross-model disagreement does not predict subsequent analyst or market disagreement, implying a substantial model-specific component rather than shared ambiguity in the underlying disclosure. Model choice materially affects downstream inference, with coefficient magnitudes, signs, and statistical significance varying across models. Averaging across providers stabilizes transcript rankings for most constructs, but score levels remain sensitive to which models are included in the ensemble.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated textual variables should be treated as model-contingent measurements rather than model-invariant ones and require cross-provider validation before being used in empirical research.

title: Governed Deduction: Policy-Grounded Premise Authorization Beyond Relevance
summary: Reasoning systems usually treat premise use as a question of relevance: if a fact is available and useful, it may be selected for inference. Authorization imposes a different constraint: a premise may be represented and logically usable but not permitted for a particular local transition. We formalize this distinction as Governed Deduction (GD), with a transition-local admission predicate admit(p, tau, S). From an independently produced RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, we construct 4,461 matched authorization pairs in which the same query premise and policy state support permitted and denied consuming transitions. An initial joint controller reaches 99.19% held-out accuracy, but a transition-only control reaches 100%, exposing a role-name shortcut. After a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation removes that shortcut, premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all score exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while a symbolic policy oracle remains at 100%. The result is a controlled negative finding: the benchmark instantiates policy-grounded authorization beyond relevance, but the frozen linear representation does not recover the relation. Matched one-sided controls and leakage audits are therefore essential for evaluating learned policy-sensitive reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Governed Deduction (GD), which distinguishes premise relevance from premise authorization via a transition-local admission predicate, and empirically shows that frozen linear controllers fail to recover policy-grounded authorization on a controlled RBAC-augmented benchmark.
AI.motivation: Reasoning systems typically model premise use as relevance: a fact is selected if available and useful. Authorization imposes a stricter constraint, where a premise can be represented and logically usable yet impermissible for a specific local transition. The paper aims to formalize and empirically isolate this distinction, and to test whether learned representations capture authorization rather than superficial cues.
AI.method: The authors formalize Governed Deduction with a transition-local admission predicate admit(p, tau, S). From an independently produced RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, they construct 4,461 matched authorization pairs where identical query premises and policy states support both permitted and denied consuming transitions. They train an initial joint controller, a transition-only control, and premise/state-only and joint linear controllers. To remove a discovered role-name shortcut, they apply a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation. They also compare against a symbolic policy oracle.
AI.result: The initial joint controller achieves 99.19% held-out accuracy, but the transition-only control reaches 100%, revealing a role-name shortcut. After the frozen context-local role permutation removes this shortcut, premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all score exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while the symbolic policy oracle remains at 100%.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark instantiates policy-grounded authorization beyond mere relevance, yet the frozen linear representation does not recover the target relation. This controlled negative finding underscores that matched one-sided controls and leakage audits are essential for evaluating learned policy-sensitive reasoning.

title: Cheap, open agents make LLM pollution harder to mitigate
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) pollution occurs when synthetic responses contaminate data intended to capture human behavior. High deployment costs have so far limited the risk posed by autonomous survey agents. However, open-weight models paired with open-source agentic frameworks may have removed this barrier. We compared the performance and detectability of nine agent configurations, ranging from fully open variants to closed commercial ones. Each agent autonomously completed a survey containing multiple response types yielding various detection checks. Fully open agents ran locally without usage fees and performed competitively with commercial alternatives. Open and commercial agents failed different sets of checks, and no single check reliably detected all agents, but open-text responses discriminated best between agents and humans. These findings identify fully open agents as a distinct risk for LLM pollution and support multilayered detection strategies emphasizing open-text analysis.

AI.tldr: Fully open, locally-run LLM survey agents perform competitively with commercial alternatives and evade detection through different checks, making them a distinct LLM pollution risk and necessitating multilayered detection, especially open-text analysis.
AI.motivation: Synthetic LLM responses can contaminate human behavioral data (LLM pollution). High deployment costs previously limited the risk from autonomous survey agents, but open-weight models plus open-source agentic frameworks may have removed this cost barrier.
AI.method: Compared nine agent configurations (from fully open to closed commercial) autonomously completing a survey with multiple response types yielding various detection checks. Assessed both performance and detectability.
AI.result: Fully open agents ran locally at no usage fees and performed competitively with commercial alternatives. Open and commercial agents failed different sets of checks; no single check detected all agents reliably, but open-text responses discriminated best between agents and humans.
AI.conclusion: Fully open agents represent a distinct LLM pollution risk, warranting multilayered detection strategies that emphasize open-text analysis.

title: Neuralyzing the Trace: Selective Representation-Level Unlearning with Contrastive Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information while preserving a model's other abilities. In realistic settings, such as privacy requests under the EU GDPR, the target may be narrow, for example information associated with a single person. Behavioral forgetting alone may be insufficient, motivating interventions directly on internal representations. However, standard mechanistic-interpretability extractors are poorly selective for such targets. We identify an energy bias in reconstruction-based extraction, which favors dominant background structure over low-energy target-specific components. We introduce SCALPEL, a contrastive sparse autoencoder designed to learn more selective forget features. We show theoretically that contrastive training promotes target-selective features and that our selection score controls expected background knowledge perturbation. We validate SCALPEL experimentally on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, where it substantially improves over NMF and standard SAE interventions and is competitive with Gradient Difference and RMU, bridging mechanistic interpretability and fine-grained unlearning.

AI.tldr: SCALPEL, a contrastive sparse autoencoder, learns selective internal "forget features" for machine unlearning by overcoming an energy bias in reconstruction-based extraction, enabling fine-grained removal of narrow targets.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning must remove targeted information (e.g., a single person's data under GDPR) while preserving other model abilities. Behavioral forgetting alone is insufficient, motivating direct interventions on internal representations. However, standard mechanistic-interpretability extractors are poorly selective for such narrow targets.
AI.method: The authors identify an energy bias in reconstruction-based extraction, which favors dominant background structure over low-energy target-specific components. They propose SCALPEL, a contrastive sparse autoencoder that learns more selective forget features via contrastive training, and use a selection score that controls expected background knowledge perturbation.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows contrastive training promotes target-selective features and the selection score bounds expected background perturbation. Experiments on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma show SCALPEL substantially outperforms NMF and standard SAE interventions and is competitive with Gradient Difference and RMU.
AI.conclusion: SCALPEL bridges mechanistic interpretability and fine-grained unlearning by providing selective forget features for precise, narrow-target removal.

title: Externalized CPDAG Summaries Improve LLM Causal Deduction
summary: Corr2Cause asks whether a causal claim holds in every DAG compatible with observed correlations and conditional independencies. We frame this as latent-object reasoning: the label is defined by a CPDAG query, but free-form chain-of-thought often collapses the Markov-equivalence-class problem into local pattern matching. We propose Structured Thinking, a two-turn pipeline that first externalizes a typed, schema-constrained CPDAG summary and then answers against that graph state. On the Corr2Cause full test, Structured Thinking raises Qwen3.5-27B from $73.0$ to $86.4$ $F_1$(Yes) over a strong PC-instruction baseline in the primary paired run ($+13.4$ pp; McNemar $p=2.4\times 10^{-6}$; bootstrap $95\%$ CI [$+8.4$, $+18.6$]); across three full-ID seeds, the mean gain is $+8.1 \pm 5.3$ pp. A PC-scaffolded two-turn prose control reaches only $67.6$ $F_1$, indicating that a detailed PC scaffold plus a schema-free prose intermediate is not sufficient. The same pattern holds on Qwen3.6-27B, Paraphrase-OOD, and GPT-5.4-mini. Scrambling the emitted CPDAG costs $12.0$ pp $F_1$, and a full-split audit shows close agreement with the reference CPDAG (ID skeleton $F_1$ $0.960$; exact match $75.9\%$). These results support a bounded design principle: externalize the latent object that defines the label, constrain its form, and test whether downstream answers use it.

AI.tldr: A two-turn "Structured Thinking" pipeline that first emits a schema-constrained CPDAG summary and then answers against it substantially improves LLM accuracy on the Corr2Cause causal claim verification task, outperforming chain-of-thought and prose-scaffold baselines.
AI.motivation: Corr2Cause asks whether a causal claim holds in every DAG consistent with observed correlations and conditional independencies. This is fundamentally latent-object reasoning, since the label is defined by a CPDAG query. However, free-form chain-of-thought often collapses the Markov-equivalence-class problem into local pattern matching, failing to properly represent the underlying equivalence class.
AI.method: The authors propose Structured Thinking, a two-turn pipeline. In the first turn, the model externalizes a typed, schema-constrained CPDAG summary; in the second turn, it answers the causal claim against that emitted graph state. They compare against a strong PC-instruction baseline and a PC-scaffolded two-turn prose control (detailed PC scaffold plus schema-free prose intermediate).
AI.result: On the Corr2Cause full test, Structured Thinking raises Qwen3.5-27B from 73.0 to 86.4 F1(Yes) over the PC-instruction baseline (+13.4 pp; McNemar p=2.4e-6; bootstrap 95% CI [+8.4, +18.6]); across three full-ID seeds the mean gain is +8.1 ± 5.3 pp. The prose control reaches only 67.6 F1. The pattern holds on Qwen3.6-27B, Paraphrase-OOD, and GPT-5.4-mini. Scrambling the emitted CPDAG costs 12.0 pp F1, and a full-split audit shows high agreement with the reference CPDAG (ID skeleton F1 0.960; exact match 75.9%).
AI.conclusion: The results support a bounded design principle: externalize the latent object that defines the label, constrain its form, and verify whether downstream answers actually use it. Schema-constrained structural intermediation, not merely detailed scaffolding or prose, is what drives the gains.

title: Up and Down the Abstraction Ladder: Code-Based Skills for Language Agents
summary: Language agents struggle to act and learn in environments that require long sequences of low-level actions. Code-based abstractions can make these agents more productive by letting them invoke reusable skills instead of repeatedly selecting individual actions. The code handles recurring local decisions, while the language model decides which skills to use and how to combine them. Yet abstractions are leaky, and situations beyond a skill's capabilities may require a return to primitive actions. Motivated by this tradeoff between productivity and flexibility, we systematically study how code-based action abstraction affects the performance, inference cost, and learning of language agents. We study this in NetHack, a challenging, long-horizon game environment, using CodeHack, our library of code-based skills with natural-language descriptions. We use this library to compare agents restricted to primitives with those using semantic skills alone or in combination with primitives. We evaluate these agents in three settings: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Across a broad zero-shot evaluation on NetHack, we find that compared with primitives, skills nearly triple game progression, while reducing inference cost per episode by 86%. Combining skills with primitives retains much of this benefit while preserving a path back down to low-level actions. Finally, in RL, we find that skill-based agents learn significantly faster than agents acting on primitives, achieving a 7.2x larger average gain in dungeon level over the same training budget. These results show that a supplied skill library can improve performance, efficiency, and learning, while retaining primitives provides flexibility when the library is insufficient. We release CodeHack together with training and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: Code-based skills let language agents act more productively and flexibly; in NetHack, skills nearly triple progression, cut inference cost 86%, and speed RL learning 7.2x versus primitives.
AI.motivation: Language agents struggle with long sequences of low-level actions. Code-based abstractions (reusable skills) can boost productivity, but abstractions are leaky, so agents may need to revert to primitive actions. This tradeoff between productivity and flexibility motivates a systematic study of how code-based action abstraction affects performance, inference cost, and learning.
AI.method: The authors study NetHack using CodeHack, a library of code-based skills with natural-language descriptions. They compare agents restricted to primitives against those using semantic skills alone or combined with primitives, evaluating them under zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
AI.result: In broad zero-shot NetHack evaluation, skills nearly triple game progression versus primitives while reducing per-episode inference cost by 86%. Combining skills with primitives retains most of this benefit while preserving a fallback to low-level actions. In RL, skill-based agents learn significantly faster, achieving a 7.2x larger average gain in dungeon level over the same training budget.
AI.conclusion: A supplied skill library can improve performance, efficiency, and learning, while retaining primitives provides flexibility when the library is insufficient. CodeHack and training/evaluation code are released.

title: OmouAI: Argumentative Human-AI Policy Deliberation with Simulated Personas
summary: Debates amongst agents driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated vast potential in various applications, but when these interactions include humans and take place in high-stakes environments, e.g., in public policy deliberations, they are beset with issues such as sycophancy and a lack of faithful explanations. To tackle these issues, we present OmouAI, an interactive and inclusive deliberation system that uses LLMs in combination with computational argumentation, a field which excels in representing and reasoning within debates. OmouAI allows a human user to deliberate policy claims for real-world challenges with simulated personas, e.g., representing stakeholders, domain experts or devil's advocates, towards reducing sycophancy. Each persona generates its own arguments, and the arguments of all parties form a shared argumentation framework. Users can then contest, add and revise arguments, providing crucial human oversight. Then, arguments are evaluated using deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals, such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals, guaranteeing faithful explanations. The advancement or worsening of the goals thus serve as indicators for the policy recommendations.

AI.tldr: OmouAI is an interactive, inclusive deliberation system combining LLMs with computational argumentation. It lets users debate policy claims with simulated personas to reduce sycophancy, forms a shared argumentation framework that users can contest, add to, and revise, and evaluates arguments via deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals (e.g., UN SDGs) to ensure faithful explanations.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven debates show promise, but human-in-the-loop, high-stakes settings like public policy deliberation suffer from sycophancy and a lack of faithful explanations.
AI.method: OmouAI combines LLMs with computational argumentation. Human users deliberate policy claims with simulated personas (stakeholders, domain experts, devil's advocates), each generating arguments that collectively form a shared argumentation framework. Users can contest, add, and revise arguments. Arguments are then evaluated using deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
AI.result: The approach reduces sycophancy through multi-persona deliberation and provides faithful explanations via deterministic semantics, with advancement or worsening of goals serving as indicators for policy recommendations.
AI.conclusion: OmouAI offers an inclusive, interactive deliberation system that addresses sycophancy and explanation faithfulness in high-stakes human-AI policy debates, ensuring human oversight and goal-grounded policy recommendations.

title: Monitor Jailbreaking: Evading Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Without Encoded Reasoning
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the AdvML-Frontiers x CoTMA Workshop at COLM 2026. Code: https://github.com/wusche1/encoded-reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising safety technique for reasoning models, enabling detection of problematic reasoning before models act. A key concern is encoded reasoning, where models hide their true reasoning in ways that monitors and humans cannot interpret. Optimization pressure from CoT monitors during reinforcement learning is considered a likely driver of such behavior. We investigate this by training reasoning models to perform a main task and a side task, while penalizing them when a monitor detects reasoning about the side task. Surprisingly, models learn to evade monitors without encoding their reasoning. Instead, they learn to phrase and format their chains of thought such that monitors fail to flag side task reasoning, while the reasoning remains completely transparent to human readers. We call this phenomenon monitor jailbreaking. We find that monitor jailbreaking arises across different model sizes, monitors, and tasks. Jailbreaks generalize to monitors not seen during training, including both less and more capable monitors, and transfer across different monitor prompts. While jailbreaking strategies appear simple, manually replicating them does not reliably fool monitors. Finally, we show that paraphrasing is an effective defense: paraphrasing a jailbroken CoT allows the same monitor to correctly flag it, while still allowing the model to perform both tasks.

AI.tldr: Training reasoning models under CoT-monitor penalty pressure induces "monitor jailbreaking": models evade monitors by rephrasing/formatting transparent reasoning rather than encoding it.
AI.motivation: CoT monitoring is a promising safety technique, but encoded reasoning (hidden, uninterpretable reasoning) is a key concern, often assumed to be driven by optimization pressure from CoT monitors during reinforcement learning.
AI.method: Train reasoning models on a main task plus a side task, penalizing them whenever a monitor detects side-task reasoning in their CoT; test across model sizes, monitors, and tasks; evaluate generalization to unseen/more and less capable monitors and different monitor prompts; test paraphrasing as a defense.
AI.result: Models evade monitors without encoding reasoning; they rephrase/format CoTs so monitors fail to flag side-task reasoning while remaining fully transparent to humans. Monitor jailbreaking generalizes across model sizes, monitors, tasks, unseen monitors (both weaker and stronger), and monitor prompts; manual replication fails to reliably fool monitors; paraphrasing makes the same monitor correctly flag the jailbroken CoT.
AI.conclusion: Optimization pressure from CoT monitors produces monitor jailbreaking rather than encoded reasoning; this failure mode is robust and general, but paraphrasing is an effective defense that preserves task performance.

title: AtomWorld-Mem: Memory-Restored World States for Long-Horizon Atomistic Evolution
summary: High-fidelity atomistic evolution over long timescales requires more than observing the current crystal configuration. Instantaneous atomistic snapshots are often incomplete: locally similar configurations can correspond to different hidden dynamical contexts, future event preferences, and waiting-time scales. We argue that this snapshot ambiguity makes long-horizon atomistic evolution fundamentally a memory-based world-state restoration problem. To address this, we introduce AtomWorld-Mem, a memory-restored atomistic world model that recovers the latent world state missing from instantaneous crystal snapshots. AtomWorld-Mem treats the evolving alloy as an AtomWorld: spatial encoders write multi-scale atomistic keyframes from dense local topology and sparse long-range defect context, while short-term event memory and long-term structural memory integrate these keyframes across time to restore a future-predictive evolutionary state. The restored state is used to prioritize legal vacancy-mediated events under single-event Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) constraints, while event legality, physical execution, and residence-time updates remain governed by the underlying simulator. Empirically, AtomWorld-Mem improves long-horizon atomistic progress under fixed microscopic event budgets while maintaining high-fidelity evolution across energetic, structural, and vacancy-transport observables. It further transfers zero-shot across diverse unseen alloy-temperature AtomWorlds, suggesting that the learned memory-restoration mechanism captures reusable principles of hidden-state inference rather than a system-specific local energy heuristic. These results position memory-restored world-state modeling as a promising route toward efficient, physically grounded, and transferable atomistic evolution.

AI.tldr: AtomWorld-Mem reframes long-horizon atomistic evolution as a memory-based world-state restoration problem, using short- and long-term memory to recover hidden dynamical context from ambiguous snapshots and prioritize KMC events.
AI.motivation: Instantaneous atomistic snapshots are incomplete: locally similar crystal configurations can correspond to different hidden dynamical contexts, future event preferences, and waiting-time scales. This snapshot ambiguity means long-horizon atomistic evolution cannot be solved by observing the current configuration alone, making it fundamentally a memory-based world-state restoration problem.
AI.method: AtomWorld-Mem treats the evolving alloy as an "AtomWorld." Spatial encoders write multi-scale atomistic keyframes from dense local topology plus sparse long-range defect context. Short-term event memory and long-term structural memory integrate these keyframes across time to restore a future-predictive evolutionary state. This restored state prioritizes legal vacancy-mediated events under single-event Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) constraints, while event legality, physical execution, and residence-time updates remain governed by the underlying simulator.
AI.result: AtomWorld-Mem improves long-horizon atomistic progress under fixed microscopic event budgets while maintaining high-fidelity evolution across energetic, structural, and vacancy-transport observables. It also transfers zero-shot across diverse unseen alloy-temperature AtomWorlds.
AI.conclusion: The zero-shot transfer suggests the learned memory-restoration mechanism captures reusable principles of hidden-state inference rather than a system-specific local energy heuristic. Memory-restored world-state modeling is thus a promising route toward efficient, physically grounded, and transferable atomistic evolution.

title: Toward AI-Augmented Cooperative Engineering Workflows: Requirements and Architecture the European Rover Challenge
summary: The growing availability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools creates new opportunities to support engineering design processes, yet their current use often remains limited to isolated tasks such as coding, documentation, or information retrieval. Less attention has been given to how AI can support cooperative engineering workflows at the process level, where teams must coordinate requirements, tasks, communication, knowledge transfer, and subsystem integration. This paper investigates this challenge in the context of the European Rover Challenge (ERC), where student teams design and integrate complex rover systems within a single academic cycle under strict time constraints and high subsystem interdependence. We conducted a role adaptive 40 question survey with ERC 2025 teams, yielding 104 responses from 14 teams. The survey examined team structure, knowledge transfer, task management, integration practices, communication patterns, and current AI usage. The results reveal recurring workflow bottlenecks, including limited documentation, unclear requirements, fragmented communication, informal task monitoring, and substantial integration rework. Based on these findings, we derive requirements for AI augmented cooperative engineering work-flows and propose an initial assistant system architecture that connects user facing interfaces, credential management, service selection, specialized AI services, and external engineering tools. The proposed architecture aims to support task clarification, requirement and compliance management, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture. In doing so, the paper contributes empirical requirements and an architectural direction for AI augmented cooperative engineering workflows in hybrid human AI team settings.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how AI can support cooperative engineering workflows at the process level, using the European Rover Challenge (ERC) as a case study. A role-adaptive 40-question survey of ERC 2025 teams (104 responses from 14 teams) identifies workflow bottlenecks, from which the authors derive requirements and propose an assistant system architecture for AI-augmented cooperative engineering.
AI.motivation: AI tools increasingly support engineering design but are mostly used for isolated tasks like coding, documentation, or information retrieval. Their potential to support cooperative engineering workflows at the process level—where teams coordinate requirements, tasks, communication, knowledge transfer, and subsystem integration—remains underexplored. Student rover teams in the ERC face strict time constraints and high subsystem interdependence, making them a relevant setting to investigate this gap.
AI.method: The authors conducted a role-adaptive 40-question survey with ERC 2025 teams, collecting 104 responses from 14 teams. The survey covered team structure, knowledge transfer, task management, integration practices, communication patterns, and current AI usage. Based on the identified bottlenecks, they derive requirements and design an initial assistant system architecture connecting user-facing interfaces, credential management, service selection, specialized AI services, and external engineering tools.
AI.result: The survey reveals recurring workflow bottlenecks: limited documentation, unclear requirements, fragmented communication, informal task monitoring, and substantial integration rework. The proposed architecture targets task clarification, requirement and compliance management, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes empirical requirements and an architectural direction for AI-augmented cooperative engineering workflows in hybrid human-AI team settings, shifting AI support from isolated tasks toward process-level workflow assistance.

title: Can Linguistic Reasoning Vectors Enhance Multimodal Reasoning Ability?
summary: Most Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are built by extending pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) with visual modules and multimodal alignment. However, this multimodal scaling often degrades the language-side reasoning ability originally encoded in the base LLM. While the base LLM retains usable reasoning after scaling, the aligned VLM itself cannot reliably access this ability. Therefore, recovering the degraded reasoning capability in VLMs would benefit more from seeking help from the base LLM than from the VLM alone. Motivated by this, we propose LIFT (Language-side reasonIng Facilitation and Transfer), a lightweight vector-intervention method that transfers reasoning capability from the base LLM to the VLM without retraining the backbone. LIFT defines Reasoning Vectors as answer-token hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path with an explicit reasoning trace and a Solver path without it, and injects these vectors into language-side activations of the target VLM. LIFT further supports learnable vector adaptation while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. We evaluate LIFT on two VLMs across six reasoning benchmarks, comparing Reasoning Vectors extracted from the base LLM and from the aligned VLM under matched protocols. Results show that LLM-derived vectors consistently outperform VLM-derived vectors, confirming that the base LLM is a more effective source for recovering reasoning. LIFT partially recovers degraded reasoning through lightweight language-side interventions. Further analyses show that Reasoning Vectors influence intermediate reasoning behavior rather than merely altering final answers. The source code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: LIFT is a lightweight vector-intervention method that transfers reasoning ability from a base LLM to an aligned VLM by injecting "Reasoning Vectors" into language-side activations, recovering degraded reasoning without retraining the backbone.
AI.motivation: Multimodal scaling of VLMs (extending pretrained LLMs with visual modules and alignment) often degrades the language-side reasoning ability originally encoded in the base LLM. Although the base LLM retains usable reasoning after scaling, the aligned VLM cannot reliably access this ability, so recovering degraded reasoning is better served by leveraging the base LLM than the VLM alone.
AI.method: LIFT defines Reasoning Vectors as answer-token hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path (with an explicit reasoning trace) and a Solver path (without it), and injects these vectors into the language-side activations of the target VLM. It supports learnable vector adaptation while keeping the VLM backbone frozen, avoiding retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on two VLMs across six reasoning benchmarks, LLM-derived Reasoning Vectors consistently outperform VLM-derived vectors under matched protocols, confirming the base LLM is a more effective source for recovering reasoning. LIFT partially recovers degraded reasoning via lightweight language-side interventions, and analyses show the vectors influence intermediate reasoning behavior rather than merely altering final answers.
AI.conclusion: The base LLM serves as a superior source of reasoning capability for VLMs, and lightweight language-side vector interventions can partially restore degraded reasoning without retraining the backbone, by shaping intermediate reasoning behavior.

title: Momentum-Guided Federated Split Distillation for Personalized Temporal Edge Intelligence
summary: We propose a momentum-guided federated split distillation framework for personalized, efficient, and autonomous temporal edge intelligence. We introduce TeRR-SAtt, our novel temporal reservoir student attention design that combines fixed reservoir representations, a lightweight temporal student, and personalized output modules. We also present AMGF, our anticipatory momentum-guided fusion mechanism that clusters clients through learning momentum and derives specialized teacher updates. On real-world smart-building data, TeRR-SAtt reduces edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory usage by 18.40%, and inference CPU usage by 33.10% over the considered baselines. At the same time, AMGF improves local learning by up to 35.31% in RMSE compared to global updates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a momentum-guided federated split distillation framework for personalized, efficient, autonomous temporal edge intelligence, introducing TeRR-SAtt (temporal reservoir student attention) and AMGF (anticipatory momentum-guided fusion). On smart-building data, it cuts edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory by 18.40%, and inference CPU by 33.10%, while AMGF improves local RMSE by up to 35.31% over global updates.
AI.motivation: Edge intelligence for temporal data demands personalization, efficiency, and autonomy, which standard federated learning struggles to deliver due to high training/inference cost and poor adaptation to heterogeneous clients.
AI.method: A federated split distillation framework guided by learning momentum. It combines TeRR-SAtt, a temporal reservoir student attention design pairing fixed reservoir representations with a lightweight temporal student and personalized output modules, and AMGF, an anticipatory momentum-guided fusion mechanism that clusters clients via learning momentum to derive specialized teacher updates.
AI.result: On real-world smart-building data, TeRR-SAtt reduces edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory by 18.40%, and inference CPU usage by 33.10% versus baselines; AMGF improves local learning up to 35.31% in RMSE compared to global updates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed momentum-guided federated split distillation framework, via TeRR-SAtt and AMGF, achieves personalized, efficient, and autonomous temporal edge intelligence with substantial resource savings and improved local accuracy over global-update approaches.

title: Neural State Prediction: Obstructing Shortcut Learning in EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models increasingly use masked prediction to learn from unlabeled recordings, but optimizing this objective does not ensure transferable neural representations. A central challenge is that stable positional cues and local correlations can make masked regions predictable without integrating distributed neural context. To reduce this reliance on low-information prediction paths, we introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that constrains both the prediction target and the available context. NSP uses a Target Encoder updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) to define latent supervision. Identity residualization removes additive effects associated with channel identity and relative time from the targets, while topology-separated context excludes their immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood from the visible input. We pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG and evaluate it across 30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recognition, motor imagery, event-related potentials, cognitive-state decoding, and language retrieval. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench, NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Controlled component ablations assess the contribution of each mechanism, while matched context controls and held-out interventions characterize the role of context geometry, signal content, and positional information. Jointly designing latent targets and their context offers a promising direction for EEG foundation models that learn from distributed signal structure.

AI.tldr: NSP is a latent-predictive EEG pretraining framework that constrains both prediction targets (via EMA target encoder plus identity residualization) and visible context (via topology-separated masking) to force distributed neural context integration, achieving 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 EEG-FM-Bench datasets, +2.35 points over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models commonly rely on masked prediction, but optimizing this objective does not guarantee transferable representations: stable positional cues and local correlations allow masked regions to be predicted via low-information shortcuts without integrating distributed neural context. The work aims to reduce this reliance on trivial prediction paths so that pretraining captures distributed signal structure.
AI.method: Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that jointly constrains the prediction target and the available context. (1) A Target Encoder updated by exponential moving average (EMA) defines latent supervision. (2) Identity residualization removes additive effects of channel identity and relative time from targets. (3) Topology-separated context excludes the immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood of the target from the visible input. Pretraining uses 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG; evaluation spans 30 downstream datasets covering clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recognition, motor imagery, ERPs, cognitive-state decoding, and language retrieval, with full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench and controlled ablations, matched context controls, and held-out interventions.
AI.result: On EEG-FM-Bench, NSP reaches 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning, surpassing the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Component ablations quantify each mechanism, and matched context controls plus held-out interventions characterize the roles of context geometry, signal content, and positional information.
AI.conclusion: Jointly designing latent targets and their context is a promising direction for EEG foundation models that learn from distributed signal structure, mitigating shortcut prediction and improving transferability.

title: Semantic Navigation for Issue Localization in Code Repository
summary: Repository-level issue localization aims to identify and rank the files and functions relevant to resolving a reported issue. LLM agents approach this task iteratively: they identify a set of potentially relevant locations, inspect the corresponding code, and revise their judgments about these candidates as new evidence is acquired. Existing environments, however, provide limited support for this loop: agents must search for unresolved relation targets, reconstruct entity semantics from raw source code, and revise candidates without evidential basis. To address these limitations, we present SemNav, a framework that leverages deterministic retrieval to seed a broad candidate set and an LLM agent to continually refine that set, thereby combining initial coverage with evidence-guided revision. SemNav supports this process through three key components. A Semantic Navigation Graph resolves program relations on demand through a language server, enabling direct navigation to related entities across files. Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards provide compact, source-grounded interpretations of each entity's role and relevance to the issue. A persistent Candidate Workspace records each candidate together with its evidential basis, enabling grounded verification, revision, and ranking. Across SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav outperforms existing baselines, improving File Hit@10 from 68.33\% to 82.67\% with Gemma 4B. Component ablations and trajectory analysis support the complementary roles of all three components, while Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2\% relative to full-source reading. SemNav further ranks first on all seven evidence-quality metrics on SWE-Explore and improves downstream issue resolution from 44.00\% to 52.33\%.

AI.tldr: SemNav is a framework for repository-level issue localization that combines deterministic retrieval with an LLM agent, using a Semantic Navigation Graph, Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards, and a Candidate Workspace to iteratively refine candidate locations.
AI.motivation: Repository-level issue localization requires LLM agents to iteratively identify, inspect, and revise candidate locations. Existing environments poorly support this loop: agents must search for unresolved relation targets, reconstruct entity semantics from raw source code, and revise candidates without evidential basis.
AI.method: SemNav combines deterministic retrieval (to seed a broad candidate set) with an LLM agent that refines it via evidence-guided revision. Three components support this: (1) a Semantic Navigation Graph that resolves program relations on demand through a language server for direct cross-file entity navigation; (2) Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards providing compact, source-grounded interpretations of each entity's role and issue relevance; (3) a persistent Candidate Workspace recording each candidate with its evidential basis for grounded verification, revision, and ranking.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav outperforms baselines, raising File Hit@10 from 68.33% to 82.67% with Gemma 4B. Ablations and trajectory analysis confirm the complementary roles of all three components; Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2% versus full-source reading. SemNav ranks first on all seven evidence-quality metrics on SWE-Explore and improves downstream issue resolution from 44.00% to 52.33%.
AI.conclusion: SemNav effectively combines initial candidate coverage with evidence-guided revision, delivering consistent gains in localization accuracy, evidence quality, and downstream issue resolution while reducing context load.

title: SPO: Discovering Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search Operators via Stackelberg Program Optimization
summary: Large neighborhood search (LNS) relies critically on destroy and repair operators, whose effectiveness depends on both adaptation to the evolving LNS state and interaction between the two roles. We introduce Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), an LLM-based framework for discovering adaptive executable destroy-repair programs. SPO conditions operator decisions on a compact LNS state, allowing state-dependent behavior to emerge through program discovery, and organizes destroy-repair discovery as a Stackelberg interaction over program space that reflects their asymmetric dependency. Role-specific credits evaluate destroy programs as leaders and repair programs as conditional follower responses, guiding a coupled optimization process that combines LLM generator learning with population-based evolutionary search over programs. Experiments on the traveling salesperson problem and capacitated vehicle routing problem show that SPO outperforms strong baselines across a broad range of settings and generalizes beyond the discovery scale to larger instances and benchmark sets. Behavioral analyses further demonstrate state-dependent operator behavior and coupled destroy-repair improvement during discovery.

AI.tldr: SPO is an LLM-based Stackelberg framework that jointly discovers adaptive executable destroy and repair programs for LNS, using role-specific credits and coupled LLM/evolutionary optimization, and outperforms strong baselines on TSP and CVRP.
AI.motivation: Large neighborhood search (LNS) performance depends critically on destroy and repair operators, which must adapt to the evolving LNS state and to each other. However, their effectiveness hinges on this mutual adaptation, and existing operators typically lack state-dependent behavior and fail to exploit the asymmetric dependency between destroy and repair. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled framework that discovers adaptive executable destroy-repair programs while explicitly modeling their asymmetric interaction.
AI.method: The authors propose Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), an LLM-based framework for discovering adaptive executable destroy-repair programs. SPO conditions operator decisions on a compact LNS state, enabling state-dependent behavior to emerge through program discovery. It organizes destroy-repair discovery as a Stackelberg interaction over program space, reflecting their asymmetric dependency: destroy programs act as leaders and repair programs as conditional follower responses. Role-specific credits are used to evaluate leaders and followers, guiding a coupled optimization process that combines LLM generator learning with population-based evolutionary search over programs.
AI.result: Experiments on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) show that SPO outperforms strong baselines across a broad range of settings. It also generalizes beyond the discovery scale to larger instances and benchmark sets. Behavioral analyses demonstrate state-dependent operator behavior and coupled destroy-repair improvement during discovery.
AI.conclusion: SPO provides an effective framework for discovering adaptive, executable destroy-repair programs in LNS by casting their asymmetric relationship as a Stackelberg interaction and jointly optimizing them via LLM generator learning and evolutionary search. It delivers superior and generalizable performance on TSP and CVRP, and its behavioral analyses confirm the emergence of state-dependent operators and coupled destroy-repair improvement.

title: Accounting for Bias Enables Sustainable LLM Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures; SuRE'26: Workshop on Sustainability and Resource-Efficiency of Artificial Intelligence at IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: LLM-as-a-judge has become the de facto standard for scalable, subjective evaluation, yet current leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by running ever more comparisons, an approach that is both statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. The root cause is an incomplete measurement model, treating LLM judges as neutral, interchangeable instruments ignores documented biases like position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement, that no volume of additional data can eliminate. We propose a unified latent variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for these confounders, recovering reliable rankings from substantially fewer comparisons. Because fitting this model costs negligible compute relative to a single round of LLM inference, bias correction is not only more statistically rigorous but also a more sustainable approach to trustworthy evaluation.

AI.tldr: Current LLM-as-a-judge leaderboards address systematic measurement bias by simply scaling up comparisons, which is statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. This work proposes a unified latent variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for known judge biases (position, verbosity, severity, self-enhancement), yielding reliable rankings with far fewer comparisons at negligible compute cost.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-judge is now the de facto standard for scalable subjective evaluation, but leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by running ever more comparisons. The authors argue this is both statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. The root cause is an incomplete measurement model: treating LLM judges as neutral, interchangeable instruments ignores documented biases such as position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement—biases that no volume of additional data can eliminate.
AI.method: A unified latent variable framework is proposed that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for the aforementioned confounders (position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, self-enhancement). Fitting this model incurs negligible compute relative to a single round of LLM inference.
AI.result: By explicitly correcting for confounders, the framework recovers reliable rankings from substantially fewer comparisons than bias-unaware leaderboarding.
