Because fitting the model is computationally negligible compared with one round of LLM inference, bias correction is achieved at minimal cost.
AI.conclusion: Bias correction via a unified latent variable framework is not only more statistically rigorous than brute-force scaling of comparisons but also a more sustainable approach to trustworthy evaluation of LLM judges.

title: Evolutionary Safety of Recursive Self-Improving AI: Taxonomy, Risk Discovery, and Evaluation
summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, with increasingly capable systems taking larger roles in reasoning, decision-making, scientific discovery, and autonomous development. As AI begins to participate in its own improvement, from model training and experience accumulation to agent evolution and automated AI development, the prospect of recursive self-improvement (RSI) is becoming increasingly relevant. This transition raises a fundamental safety question: how can safety be maintained when the system, its accumulated experience, and even the process producing its successors continue to change?
  We introduce Evolutionary Safety as a perspective for studying safety under persistent and recursive self-improvement. It concerns not only whether an AI system is safe at a particular moment, but how safety properties change, persist, accumulate, and propagate throughout evolution. We characterize recurring manifestations, including intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, and risk propagation. We then develop a taxonomy spanning persistent agent state, model state, evaluation and environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms. Building on this taxonomy, we examine how evolutionary risks can be discovered and evaluated across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages, and derive governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery. Finally, we outline open problems toward maintaining safety guarantees as AI systems become increasingly persistent, adaptive, and recursively self-improving. Project resources and proposed evaluation systems are available at https://chaunceykung.github.io/evolutionary-safety-rsi.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Evolutionary Safety," a framework for studying how safety properties change, persist, accumulate, and propagate under recursive self-improvement (RSI), and lays out a taxonomy, evaluation approach, and governance principles.
AI.motivation: AI systems are taking larger roles in reasoning, decision-making, scientific discovery, and autonomous development, and are increasingly participating in their own improvement (model training, experience accumulation, agent evolution, automated AI development). This makes recursive self-improvement increasingly relevant and raises a fundamental safety question: how safety can be maintained when the system, its accumulated experience, and even the process producing its successors keep changing.
AI.method: The authors introduce Evolutionary Safety as a perspective for safety under persistent and recursive self-improvement. They characterize recurring manifestations (intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, risk propagation); develop a taxonomy spanning persistent agent state, model state, evaluation and environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms; examine how evolutionary risks can be discovered and evaluated across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages; and derive governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery.
AI.result: The paper provides a characterization of recurrent evolutionary failure modes, a five-layer taxonomy of the RSI setting, an evaluation approach spanning states, updates, trajectories, and lineages, and a set of governance principles. Project resources and proposed evaluation systems are made available at the linked project page.
AI.conclusion: The paper reframes AI safety beyond point-in-time system safety toward the study of how safety properties evolve, persist, accumulate, and propagate across lineages. It outlines open problems toward maintaining safety guarantees as AI systems become increasingly persistent, adaptive, and recursively self-improving.

title: Samples, Sources, Space: Decomposing Data Scale in Spatially Structured Representation Learning of Human Brain Microarchitecture
summary: Scaling studies typically represent training data by a single count of samples. For hierarchically and spatially structured data, however, the same number of samples can be drawn from few or many sources and distributed differently across the underlying domain. We therefore study data scaling as an allocation problem, separating unique sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage. We study this decomposition in microscopic whole-brain histology, where a source is an individual brain, and a sample is an image patch at a specific spatial location. Across 93 controlled pretraining runs of a contrastive model that uses spatial proximity for supervision, we vary data allocation, compute, and model capacity over 11.6 million spatially anchored image patches from 21 human brains. Performance improves with more unique samples, broader spatial coverage, additional compute, and larger model capacity. At fixed sample count, distributing samples across one to 18 subjects produces no detectable improvement, even though representations generalize substantially better to subjects encountered during pretraining. Inter-subject variation therefore strongly affects generalization, but additional subjects provide no benefit when a fixed sample budget is distributed across more sources. These results establish sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage as distinct axes of data scaling in spatially structured representation learning.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes data scaling for hierarchically and spatially structured data as an allocation problem separating unique sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage, and tests it via 93 controlled contrastive pretraining runs on whole-brain histology.
AI.motivation: Standard scaling studies collapse training data into a single sample count, which is inadequate for structured data where the same number of samples can come from few or many sources and be spread unevenly across the underlying domain. The authors want to disentangle whether gains come from more samples, more sources, or broader spatial coverage.
AI.method: They decompose data scaling into unique sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage, and study it in microscopic whole-brain histology where a source is an individual brain and a sample is an image patch at a specific spatial location. Using spatially anchored image patches, they run 93 controlled pretraining experiments with a contrastive model supervised by spatial proximity, varying data allocation, compute, and model capacity across 11.6 million image patches drawn from 21 human brains.
AI.result: Performance improves with more unique samples, broader spatial coverage, additional compute, and larger model capacity. At a fixed sample count, distributing samples across one to 18 subjects yields no detectable improvement, even though representations generalize substantially better to subjects seen during pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Inter-subject variation strongly affects generalization, yet adding more subjects gives no benefit when a fixed sample budget is spread across more sources. Sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage are thus distinct axes of data scaling in spatially structured representation learning.

title: Which Influence Are We Estimating? The Role of Counterfactual Specifications in Data Attribution
summary: Estimating the influence of training examples on model behavior is essential for data debugging, valuation, and attribution. Existing influence estimators often produce incompatible rankings, which are commonly ascribed to approximation error. We argue that a more fundamental source of disagreement is specification mismatch: influence depends on the behavior being attributed, the intervention applied to each training example, and the counterfactual training process that maps the intervention to a model response. These choices are especially important when the target behavior requires a tractable surrogate, such as query loss, a logit, or a margin. We formalize influence as a counterfactual estimand, distinguish specification mismatch across estimands from approximation error in estimating a fixed estimand, and organize representative estimators by their implied specifications. We further derive a local decomposition that exposes how behavior signals, training signals, and counterfactual parameter responses interact. Controlled experiments show that exact estimands under different specifications can induce different rankings, whereas approximation error grows as perturbations move farther from their linearization points. Experiments on noisy label detection and LLM attribution show that specification choices significantly affect attribution quality, especially for the choice of behavior surrogate. Behavior-aligned specifications can identify target-specific training examples obscured by default loss-based or similarity-based specifications. These results establish specification analysis as a necessary first step for interpreting and comparing data influence estimators.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that disagreements between data influence estimators stem not mainly from approximation error but from specification mismatch—differences in the target behavior, the intervention on training examples, and the counterfactual training process. The authors formalize influence as a counterfactual estimand and show that behavior-aligned specifications materially change attribution quality in noisy label detection and LLM attribution.
AI.motivation: Influence estimation is important for data debugging, valuation, and attribution, yet existing estimators frequently yield incompatible rankings. These disagreements are usually blamed on approximation error, but the authors contend that a more fundamental cause is specification mismatch, which becomes especially consequential when the target behavior must be replaced by a tractable surrogate such as query loss, a logit, or a margin.
AI.method: The paper formalizes influence as a counterfactual estimand and separates two issues: specification mismatch across estimands versus approximation error in estimating a fixed estimand. It organizes representative estimators according to their implied specifications and derives a local decomposition that exposes interactions among behavior signals, training signals, and counterfactual parameter responses. Controlled experiments and applications to noisy label detection and LLM attribution are used to test these claims.
AI.result: Exact estimands under different specifications can produce different rankings, while approximation error grows as perturbations move farther from their linearization points. Specification choices, especially the behavior surrogate, significantly affect attribution quality; behavior-aligned specifications uncover target-specific training examples that default loss-based or similarity-based specifications obscure.
AI.conclusion: Specification analysis should be treated as a necessary first step for interpreting and comparing data influence estimators, since specification mismatch is a first-order source of disagreement distinct from approximation error.

title: DIAL: Position-Debiased LLM Judges with Adaptive Human Preference Calibration
summary: Large language models (LLMs) as a judge enable scalable evaluation, but their judgments can be sensitive to response order and, even after removing such position effects, can still diverge systematically from human preferences.We introduce DIAL, a unified framework that combines abundant LLM comparisons with limited human comparisons to separate judge-specific position effects, learn shared structure in position-debiased LLM preferences, and adaptively calibrate that structure toward the human preference target. Theoretically, we study three aspects of DIAL: (i) identification of latent LLM preferences, position effects, and human calibration; (ii) adaptive estimation that balances LLM anchoring against limited human evidence; and (iii) fixed-weight uncertainty quantification for the calibrated human preference. Empirically, we evaluate position debiasing and human alignment separately in controlled simulations and on three human-preference benchmarks, showing that DIAL remains robust to unbalanced response order, achieves strong human-aligned rankings with limited labels, and adapts toward human evidence when LLM information is imperfect. Our real-data study collects over 410K judgments from 21 LLM judges in both display orders, providing a resource for future studies of LLM-judge bias, heterogeneity, and human alignment.

AI.tldr: DIAL is a unified framework that combines abundant LLM comparisons with limited human comparisons to separate judge-specific position effects, learn shared structure in position-debiased LLM preferences, and adaptively calibrate toward the human preference target.
AI.motivation: LLMs as judges enable scalable evaluation, but their judgments are sensitive to response order, and even after removing position effects they can still diverge systematically from human preferences. A method is needed to jointly handle position bias and human alignment under limited human labels.
AI.method: DIAL combines abundant LLM comparisons with limited human comparisons. It separates judge-specific position effects, learns shared structure in position-debiased LLM preferences, and adaptively calibrates that structure toward the human preference target. The theory covers identification, adaptive estimation balancing LLM anchoring against limited human evidence, and fixed-weight uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Evaluated in controlled simulations and on three human-preference benchmarks: DIAL remains robust to unbalanced response order, achieves strong human-aligned rankings with limited labels, and adapts toward human evidence when LLM information is imperfect. The real-data study collects over 410K judgments from 21 LLM judges in both display orders.
AI.conclusion: DIAL provides a unified approach to debiasing LLM judges for position effects while calibrating to human preferences, and the collected dataset offers a resource for future studies of LLM-judge bias, heterogeneity, and human alignment.

title: Purin: A Biology-inspired Mechanism for Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) usually represent neural transmission with fixed trainable weights during a training batch, which omits short-term changes in synaptic efficacy. In addition, the discrete time-step simulation requires additional temporal processing that many conventional ANN architectures do not use. To overcome these challenges, we propose Purin, a biology-inspired and ANN-compatible mechanism, that introduces synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional convolutional neural networks. Purin uses a time-interval-based abstraction for neural activities, which allows Purin to introduce short- and long-term synaptic efficacy changes without using discrete time-steps. Purin introduces a bounded factor to represent temporary synaptic efficacy changes, together with two weight matrices that represent input-side and output-side efficacy. The weight matrices are updated by backpropagation and interpreted as the long-term synaptic efficacy changes. Experimental results show that after removing the confounding factors in the AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet architectures, Purin improves the classification accuracies in all three models across the evaluated datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Purin, a biology-inspired yet ANN-compatible mechanism that introduces short- and long-term synaptic efficacy modulation into standard CNNs via a time-interval-based abstraction, yielding improved classification accuracy without discrete time-step simulation.
AI.motivation: Conventional ANNs model neural transmission with fixed trainable weights during a training batch, thereby omitting short-term changes in synaptic efficacy. Moreover, discrete time-step simulation demands additional temporal processing that many standard ANN architectures do not support. These limitations motivate a mechanism that captures dynamic synaptic efficacy while remaining compatible with existing convolutional networks.
AI.method: Purin adopts a time-interval-based abstraction for neural activities, enabling short- and long-term synaptic efficacy changes without discrete time-steps. It introduces a bounded factor representing temporary (short-term) synaptic efficacy changes, together with two weight matrices encoding input-side and output-side efficacy. These weight matrices are updated via backpropagation and interpreted as long-term synaptic efficacy changes.
AI.result: After removing confounding factors in the AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet architectures, Purin improves classification accuracy across all three models on the evaluated datasets.
AI.conclusion: Purin offers a practical, ANN-compatible route to incorporating biologically inspired synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional CNNs, demonstrating consistent accuracy gains and providing a foundation for further exploration of dynamic synaptic behavior in deep learning.

title: MA-WAM: Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Test-Time Planning
comment: 40 pages, including appendices. Project page: https://ma-wam.github.io/
summary: Multi-agent cooperative tasks require different agents to execute a joint action simultaneously, and each agent's action affects both the observations and responses of the other agents. Hence, a world model is needed to predict the team return resulting from the joint actions of all agents. A naive extension directly applies a single-agent world model to each agent's action when predicting the team return step by step. However, such an extension fails to capture the dependencies among the simultaneous actions of multiple agents. We propose Multi-Agent World-Action Model (MA-WAM), a test-time planning framework that enables a frozen multi-agent flow policy to evaluate futures of candidate joint actions. To our knowledge, MA-WAM is the first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies. MA-WAM predicts the consequences of each joint action according to cross-agent dependencies and enables efficient candidate scoring. Across 30 offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) settings on MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE, MA-WAM achieves mean relative gains of 22.0% over direct execution and 25.6% over uniform action selection. Under the standard evaluation protocol on an A100 GPU, MA-WAM adds 12.1 ms, accounting for 2.5% of the measured generation-and-scoring time.

AI.tldr: MA-WAM is the first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies, predicting joint-action consequences via cross-agent dependencies to score candidate joint actions efficiently.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent cooperative tasks require agents to execute joint actions simultaneously, where each agent's action affects others' observations and responses. A world model is thus needed to predict team return from joint actions of all agents. Naively applying a single-agent world model per agent fails to capture dependencies among simultaneous actions.
AI.method: MA-WAM: a test-time planning framework enabling a frozen multi-agent flow policy to evaluate futures of candidate joint actions. It predicts consequences of each joint action according to cross-agent dependencies and enables efficient candidate scoring.
AI.result: Across 30 offline MARL settings on MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE, MA-WAM achieves mean relative gains of 22.0% over direct execution and 25.6% over uniform action selection. On an A100 GPU, it adds 12.1 ms, only 2.5% of the measured generation-and-scoring time.
AI.conclusion: MA-WAM is the first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies, effectively capturing cross-agent dependencies in joint actions with high efficiency and significant performance gains.

title: G2MAF: Test-Time Gradient Guidance for Multi-Agent Flow Policies
comment: 24 pages, including appendices. Project page: https://g2maf.github.io/
summary: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) learns cooperative policies from fixed datasets without further environment interaction and a learned policy is frozen at deployment. Such a frozen policy typically proposes a single joint action and executes it directly at deployment time. However, this one-shot deployment often commits to a suboptimal proposal, even when better nearby alternatives remain consistent with the behavior data. To address this issue, we propose Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow (G2MAF), a refinement framework for optimizing joint policies at test-time. G2MAF applies one globally normalized, projected critic gradient to guide and coordinate all agents' corrections while keeping the action both feasible and close to the frozen policy proposal. Across 24 MPE and SMAC settings, its canonical variant improves 20 frozen settings, with mean relative gains of 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC, with model inference latency increased by about 6% only.

AI.tldr: G2MAF is a test-time refinement framework for offline MARL that uses a single globally normalized, projected critic gradient to coordinate all agents' corrections, improving 20 of 24 frozen MPE/SMAC settings with ~9% relative gains at ~6% extra inference latency.
AI.motivation: Offline MARL learns cooperative policies from fixed datasets without further environment interaction, and the learned policy is frozen at deployment. A frozen policy typically proposes a single joint action executed directly, which often commits to a suboptimal proposal even when better nearby alternatives remain consistent with the behavior data.
AI.method: G2MAF (Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow) is a refinement framework for optimizing joint policies at test time. It applies one globally normalized, projected critic gradient to guide and coordinate all agents' corrections, while keeping the action both feasible and close to the frozen policy proposal.
AI.result: Across 24 MPE and SMAC settings, the canonical variant of G2MAF improves 20 frozen settings, achieving mean relative gains of 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC, with model inference latency increased by only about 6%.
AI.conclusion: Test-time joint-policy refinement via a globally normalized, projected critic gradient can substantially improve frozen offline MARL policies at minimal computational cost.

title: The Right Information Extraction Pipeline Depends on the Document: Accuracy-Energy Trade-offs for Small, Local Models
summary: Whether an information extraction pipeline should process page images or parsed text depends on the document, and the answer flips across the layout spectrum. We study this trade-off under a constraint that rules out (closed) cloud services: privacy-sensitive documents processed on-premise by small ($\le 8\mathrm{B}$ parameter) text-only and vision--language models, evaluated on both accuracy and energy over a design space spanning input representation, model family, and inference configuration. Benchmarking on the near-plain-text Kleister-NDA contracts and the layout-rich VRDU forms, we find that batching is the dominant energy lever, cutting energy per page by 38-85% at no cost in accuracy, while FP8 quantization saves 27-32% when requests are served one at a time but less than 1mWh per page (9-19%) once batching is applied. Preprocessing dominates what remains: neural OCR costs $17\times$ more energy per page than classical OCR and never reaches the Pareto frontier. Which representation wins flips with the type of document: vision--language models on layout-rich documents and small text-only models with a cheap parser on near-plain text, where they are both more accurate and cheaper than any vision--language configuration. Our work yields concrete guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local information extraction.

AI.tldr: Under an on-premise, privacy-compliant constraint with small (≤8B) models, batching is the dominant energy lever (38-85% savings at no accuracy cost), preprocessing dominates remaining energy (neural OCR is 17× costlier than classical and never Pareto-optimal), and the winning input representation flips by document type: vision-language models for layout-rich documents, cheap-parser text-only models for near-plain text.
AI.motivation: Whether an information extraction pipeline should use page images or parsed text depends on the document, and the answer flips across the layout spectrum. The trade-off is studied under a constraint that rules out closed cloud services: privacy-sensitive documents must be processed on-premise by small (≤8B parameter) text-only and vision-language models, so accuracy must be balanced against energy cost.
AI.method: A design-space study spanning input representation, model family, and inference configuration, evaluated on both accuracy and energy. Small (≤8B) text-only and vision-language models are benchmarked under on-premise, privacy-compliant constraints, using near-plain-text Kleister-NDA contracts and layout-rich VRDU forms.
AI.result: Batching is the dominant energy lever, cutting energy per page by 38-85% at no accuracy cost. FP8 quantization saves 27-32% when requests are served one at a time, but less than 1 mWh per page (9-19%) once batching is applied. Preprocessing dominates the remainder: neural OCR costs 17× more energy per page than classical OCR and never reaches the Pareto frontier. The winning representation flips with document type: vision-language models on layout-rich documents, and small text-only models with a cheap parser on near-plain text, where they are both more accurate and cheaper than any vision-language configuration.
AI.conclusion: The work yields concrete guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local information extraction.

title: Mutable Transcripts: Mitigating Context Pollution through Editable Conversation State
summary: Contemporary large language model (LLM) chat systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence of turns that defines the model's working context. However, user intent in real interactions is not static: it evolves through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints. This mismatch between dynamic intent and static transcripts can result in context pollution, where outdated or irrelevant information persists and continues to influence subsequent responses. We introduce mutable transcripts, a new interaction paradigm that enables users to revise prior turns through natural language edit requests, allowing the conversation history itself to be updated rather than appended. This reframes the transcript from a passive record into an editable representation of conversational state. We present a working prototype that integrates transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface and evaluate its feasibility through a controlled user study (n=17) and an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios. Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat across measures of clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis of representative user study conversations shows that mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context. These findings provide initial evidence that user-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and help maintain a more current representation of user intent. The source code and prototype can be accessed at https://github.com/QxLabIreland/ReChat

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "mutable transcripts," an interaction paradigm allowing users to revise prior conversation turns via natural language edit requests, so chat history is updated rather than appended. A prototype was evaluated in a controlled user study (n=17) and transcript analysis, showing strong preference over standard chat and reduced conversation length and obsolete context.
AI.motivation: LLM chat systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence of turns defining the working context, but user intent is dynamic—evolving through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints. This mismatch causes context pollution: outdated or irrelevant information persists and keeps influencing later responses.
AI.method: The authors propose mutable transcripts, which let users revise prior turns through natural-language edit requests, reframing the transcript from a passive record into an editable representation of conversational state. They build a working prototype integrating transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface, and evaluate it through a controlled user study (n=17) plus an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios.
AI.result: Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat on clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis showed mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context.
AI.conclusion: User-driven revision of conversational history offers initial evidence of improving interaction quality and maintaining a more current representation of user intent. Source code and prototype are available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
summary: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way: using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with a system they call program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. We reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic MCTS in more detail than the original paper and applied it across 5 models. We reproduced several of PoLar's findings: skipping outperformed the standard pass, repeating outperformed skipping, and combining both outperformed either alone. Shorter programs sufficed for easier questions, while harder questions required more layer repeats. However, we failed to replicate the main claim regarding their learned router for single-shot inference: its top-ranked prediction consistently collapsed back to the standard pass, even though its top-k predicted programs, taken together, did show a real accuracy gain. Beyond reproduction, we find that a small number of generic programs are enough to solve most of the questions. We also provide a much deeper analysis of these programs' structure and robustness: for example, we found that programs that correct errors are highly brittle: undoing even a single edit inside a program typically breaks the correction. Connecting this to the brain's routing mechanisms, PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers. We publicly release the code at https://datexis.github.io/RE-PoLar/

AI.tldr: This paper reproduces and extends PoLar, which treats transformer layers as a callable function library for adaptive layer routing. It confirms skipping/repeating benefits but fails to replicate the learned single-shot router's main claim, and finds only a few generic programs suffice while error-correcting programs are highly brittle.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM inference is a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass regardless of input difficulty, unlike the brain's thalamus-mediated flexible routing. PoLar proposed giving transformers similar flexibility by treating layers as a function library, but its diagnostic MCTS and learned router lacked detailed independent verification.
AI.method: Reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic MCTS in greater detail than the original work and applied it across 5 models. Tested layer skipping, repeating, and combined programs; examined program length vs. question difficulty; evaluated the learned router for single-shot inference; analyzed program structure, genericity, and robustness (edit-based brittleness), and drew parallels to thalamo-cortical coordination.
AI.result: Reproduced several PoLar findings: skipping outperformed the standard pass, repeating outperformed skipping, and combining both outperformed either alone. Shorter programs sufficed for easier questions, while harder questions required more repeats. Failed to replicate the main router claim: its top-1 prediction collapsed to the standard pass, though top-k predicted programs collectively yielded a real accuracy gain. A small number of generic programs solved most questions. Error-correcting programs were highly brittle—undoing a single edit typically broke the correction.
AI.conclusion: PoLar's layer-routing flexibility is partly reproducible, but the learned single-shot router's top-1 behavior does not hold up; gains persist only when aggregating top-k programs. The approach mirrors thalamo-cortical routing principles, and code is publicly released at https://datexis.github.io/RE-PoLar/.

title: Completed Pairs Hide Capped Failures: A ReVerPi Case Study of Selective Context Projection
comment: 15 pages, 12 tables, 5 figures. Project code: https://github.com/timwhitez/ReVer_Pi. Source archive includes anc/ analysis data and reproduction scripts
summary: Context projection replaces older tool observations with compact, addressable excerpts, reducing repeated input while potentially adding evidence-retrieval turns. We study this trade-off in ReVerPi, a Pi extension with archived observations and matched full/projected continuations. In an 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests, the 15 completed pairs show identical success: 12/15 per arm. Twelve further boundary runs stop, with the runner suppressing the companion whenever the first arm fails to complete. Restoring all 27 boundary runs bounds projected-minus-full success between $-$9 and +1 tasks. title: Compress What You See, Not What You Say: Anchored Context Distillation for Latent-Observation Software Engineering Agents
summary: Tool observations dominate the context of software-engineering agents, making long interaction histories costly to maintain. Existing context compression methods can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior. To reduce context while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior, we combine Latent Observations, Hard Actions (LOHA), a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference, with Anchored Context Distillation (ACD), a training method that enables latent reading while constraining behavioral drift. LOHA compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text, providing compact access to historical information and exact access to recent content. To enable the agent to use this representation, ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring its behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model. On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for their uncompressed bases. A single-run recency sweep reaches 14.4% and 23.0% at K=8, with larger windows generally favoring task performance over compression. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. In concurrent single-GPU serving, it achieves 1.9 times that full-text agent's instance throughput.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LOHA (Latent Observations, Hard Actions) plus Anchored Context Distillation (ACD) to compress software-engineering agent context while preserving action-critical information and behavior. LOHA keeps the agent's own turns and last K observations in text, compressing older tool observations into soft tokens; ACD trains the agent to read this latent view. On SWE-bench Verified, this cuts per-call context by 43–57% with modest resolve-rate drops, and under a 32K limit yields higher resolve rates and 1.9× throughput.

Existing context compression can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior. The goal is to reduce context while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior.
AI.method: LOHA is a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference: it compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text. Anchored Context Distillation (ACD) is a training method enabling latent reading while constraining behavioral drift. ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring the agent's behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for uncompressed bases. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. AI.conclusion: LOHA with ACD reduces agent context substantially while retaining action-critical information and limiting behavioral drift, trading small losses at aggressive compression for better performance and throughput under tight token limits.

title: Segment-Level Agentic Topic Modeling for Improved Data Exploration and Resource Efficiency
summary: Topic modeling is an effective technique for discovering hidden themes within documents and is widely used in text mining and data analysis across a variety of industry sectors. Recently, large language model (LLM)-based topic models have been emerged that prompt LLMs to generate topics then assign the topics to documents, producing more natural and human-readable topics than conventional topic modeling algorithms. However, the nature of topic assignment process causes certain drawbacks, such as the incapability to produce topic distributions over a document, too broad or narrow topics, and high resource consumption, which increases with the number and length of of documents being assigned topics. These issues are particularly critical for industrial applications, which require high-quality, in-depth analysis and the processing of large volumes of documents. In this context, this paper introduces a framework called SeLATM, which addresses these concerns by employing segment-level topic generation and topic refinement through agentic feedback loops. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that SeLATM significantly reduces the LLM resources compared to methods based on topic assignment process, while maintaining superior performance.

AI.tldr: SeLATM is an LLM-based topic modeling framework that uses segment-level topic generation and agentic feedback loops for refinement, achieving high-quality topics with far lower LLM resource consumption than topic-assignment-based methods.
AI.motivation: LLM-based topic models generate more natural, human-readable topics than conventional algorithms, but their topic-assignment paradigm has drawbacks: it cannot produce topic distributions over a document, yields overly broad or narrow topics, and incurs high resource consumption that grows with the number and length of documents. These limitations are critical for industrial applications requiring high-quality, in-depth analysis of large document volumes.
AI.method: The paper proposes SeLATM, a framework that employs segment-level topic generation and topic refinement via agentic feedback loops, avoiding the topic-assignment process that causes the aforementioned issues.
AI.result: Experiments on various datasets show that SeLATM significantly reduces LLM resource usage compared to topic-assignment-based methods while maintaining superior performance.
AI.conclusion: SeLATM offers an efficient, high-quality alternative for LLM-based topic modeling, well-suited to industrial-scale, in-depth document analysis.

title: Game Arena: Strategic LLM Evaluation in Competitive Environments
comment: 31 pages, 15 figures. Technical report. Project page: https://www.kaggle.com/game-arena
summary: We introduce Kaggle Game Arena, an open and ever-expanding platform to evaluate large language models (LLMs) through competitive games. Different from static benchmarks, game arena enables models to play head-to-head matchups in structured environments where the gameplay strength naturally increases as models evolve, preventing performance saturation. This technical report details the infrastructure behind Game Arena and describes the three pilot game environments: Chess, Poker, and Werewolf. These environments span perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer game settings, enabling a systematic study of models' strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty. For each game, we provide a detailed description of the environment, evaluation metrics, and results from running full competitions across models. Through robust infrastructure and large-scale ground-truth based evaluation, Game Arena ensures reproducibility, transparency and generalizability to new games and variants over time.

AI.tldr: Kaggle Game Arena is introduced as an open, ever-expanding platform that evaluates LLMs via competitive games (Chess, Poker, Werewolf) instead of static benchmarks, enabling saturation-resistant, reproducible, and generalizable assessment of strategic reasoning under varying information settings.
AI.motivation: Static benchmarks for evaluating LLMs tend to saturate as models improve, and they fail to capture dynamic capabilities like strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty. A competitive, evolving evaluation paradigm is needed to keep pace with model progress.
AI.method: The paper presents the infrastructure behind Game Arena and three pilot game environments: Chess (perfect information), Poker (imperfect information), and Werewolf (multiplayer). For each game, it defines the environment, evaluation metrics, and runs full competitions across models, using robust infrastructure and large-scale ground-truth based evaluation.
AI.result: Full competitions were run across models in all three pilot environments, yielding model comparisons via the defined metrics. The platform demonstrates reproducibility, transparency, and generalizability to new games and variants over time.
AI.conclusion: Game Arena offers a scalable, saturation-resistant evaluation framework for LLMs based on head-to-head gameplay, spanning perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer settings, and is designed to extend to new games and variants.

title: "AI is (not) the new...": A Diagnostic Analogy Framework for Generative AI's Cultural Impacts
summary: Generative AI is reshaping the cultural infrastructures through which knowledge is found, synthesized, and held accountable. To make sense of this shift, scholars and policymakers reach for historical analogies of technologies such as the printing press, steam power or electricity. But these comparisons are typically imprecise about which property of the technology carries the comparison, and imprecise analogies produce imprecise governance by designing interventions against the wrong property of the system. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. We decompose each intervention into three coordinates: the epistemic site at which a technology acts, the governing logic by which it organizes its object, and the technical mechanism through which the logic is instantiated. This framework allows us to distinguish between structural cultural consequences, which follow from the mechanism itself, from contingent ones, which remain open to design and institutional choice. Applying the framework to information discovery and knowledge synthesis, we show how the shift from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus produces specific, traceable cultural effects and reveals governance levers that gestalt analogy obscures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-coordinate diagnostic framework—epistemic site, governing logic, and technical mechanism—to analyze how generative AI transforms epistemic and cultural practice, distinguishing structural from contingent effects and exposing governance levers that broad historical analogies obscure.
AI.motivation: Scholars and policymakers rely on historical analogies (printing press, steam power, electricity) to understand generative AI's cultural impact, but these analogies are imprecise about which technological property is being compared. Such imprecision yields misguided governance interventions targeting the wrong system property.
AI.method: The authors develop a diagnostic framework that decomposes each technological intervention into three coordinates: (1) the epistemic site at which the technology acts, (2) the governing logic by which it organizes its object, and (3) the technical mechanism instantiating that logic. They apply this framework to two domains—information discovery and knowledge synthesis—identifying shifts from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus.
AI.result: Applying the framework reveals specific, traceable cultural effects of generative AI and separates structural consequences (inherent to the mechanism) from contingent ones (open to design and institutional choice). It also identifies governance levers that gestalt-style analogies conceal.
AI.conclusion: Precise analysis of generative AI's cultural transformation requires decomposing interventions into their epistemic, logical, and technical dimensions rather than relying on imprecise historical analogies, enabling more targeted and effective governance.

title: UQ-LOB: Uncertainty-Aware Limit Order Book Mid-Price Forecasting
summary: Forecasting short-horizon mid-price movements from limit order book (LOB) data is central to algorithmic trading, yet most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors: they output a direction or a displacement, but never indicate which of their forecasts can be trusted. We introduce UQ-LOB, a lightweight, encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module that attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder and, in the spirit of attentive neural processes, conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows whose outcomes are already realised. The UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over the future tick displacement, while the UQ-classification variant outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both expose a scalar confidence (predicted signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) that supports selective prediction. On 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and horizons of 5, 10 and 15 seconds, UQ-regression attains near-nominal 68% interval coverage, and restricting to the most confident 10% of predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05-0.11 for UQ-classification, at every horizon. On large, economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches a directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at the 5-second horizon.

AI.tldr: UQ-LOB is an encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module that attaches to any pretrained limit order book encoder and conditions forecasts on a context set of realised recent windows, enabling calibrated confidence for selective prediction of short-horizon mid-price movements.
AI.motivation: Most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors that output a direction or displacement but never indicate which forecasts can be trusted, limiting their utility for risk-aware algorithmic trading.
AI.method: Inspired by attentive neural processes, UQ-LOB conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows with realised outcomes. Its UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over future tick displacement; the UQ-classification variant outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both expose a scalar confidence (predicted SNR or class probability) supporting selective prediction, and the module is lightweight and attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets at 5, 10, and 15-second horizons: UQ-regression achieves near-nominal 68% interval coverage; retaining only the top 10% most confident predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 (regression) and 0.05-0.11 (classification) at every horizon. On large economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at 5 seconds.
AI.conclusion: UQ-LOB provides calibrated, encoder-agnostic uncertainty estimates that enable effective selective prediction, concentrating accuracy on high-confidence forecasts and yielding strong directional F1 on economically significant moves.

title: Prompt Minimization: Reducing Input Redundancy Without Sacrificing Output Fidelity
summary: Despite the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc. This project will explore $\textit{prompt minimization}$, the process of reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity. Practically, shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts, such as entire documents or codebases, are included unnecessarily. Further, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, the existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests a high degree of redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors. We propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts and demonstrate that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts. These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen our understanding of input compression in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper explores "prompt minimization"—reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity—and proposes three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts.
AI.motivation: Prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc despite growing LLM capabilities. Shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency (especially when unnecessary large contexts like documents or codebases are included), and longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggest high redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors.
AI.method: The project proposes three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts, reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity.
AI.result: Minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts.
AI.conclusion: These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen understanding of input compression in LLMs.

title: A Flow Matching Framework for Neural Representational Dissimilarity
summary: Neural representational dissimilarity quantifies differences between neural response distributions, and is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. Commonly used distance metrics involve different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods. Here, we show that a variety of distance metrics can be unified under a flow matching framework developed in deep generative models. That is, these distances arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints. We find that flow matching has advantages for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables. Furthermore, this framework enables the design of new distance metrics in a principled way. Together, flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper unifies various neural representational dissimilarity metrics under a flow matching framework, showing they correspond to Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints, enabling better estimation and principled design of new metrics.
AI.motivation: Neural representational dissimilarity is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. However, commonly used distance metrics rely on different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods, lacking a unified understanding.
AI.method: The authors adopt a flow matching framework from deep generative models, demonstrating that a variety of distance metrics arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints.
AI.result: Flow matching proves advantageous for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables, and the framework enables principled design of new distance metrics.
AI.conclusion: Flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics.

title: Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are often expected to improve as team size increases, yet the scaling behavior may depend on task structure. Our central contribution is to introduce Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks as a framework for analyzing multi-agent LLM scaling and focusing the analysis on disjunctive and compensatory tasks. We model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, which yields their large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the model's modal answer, and averaging converges to the model's item-level bias. Across selected representative benchmarks, 13 open-weight models, and teams of up to 30 agents, we find qualitatively different scaling behavior. On disjunctive tasks, the probability that at least one agent is correct grows by 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting over agents that answer directly realises almost none of this potential, as the model predicts to within 0.5 points on average. Multi-round revision raises accuracy considerably, yet the gain is nearly the same with one peer as with 29. In contrast, scaling provides little benefit on Fermi estimation, despite its natural suitability for aggregation: item-level biases shared across the samples of a model account for about 87% of the squared error, so averaging reduces error by only about 6%. Combining model families helps on Fermi estimation but does not surpass the strongest member on disjunctive tasks. These results show that task structure, together with the mechanism combining member outputs, is a fundamental determinant of team scaling.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM scaling depends fundamentally on task structure (Steiner's taxonomy) and the output combination mechanism, not team size alone.
AI.motivation: Team-size scaling of multi-agent LLM systems is often assumed to improve performance, but the authors argue this depends on task structure. They introduce Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks as a principled framework to analyze when and how team scaling actually helps.
AI.method: They model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, deriving large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the modal answer; averaging converges to the item-level bias. They empirically test disjunctive and compensatory (Fermi estimation) tasks across representative benchmarks, 13 open-weight models, and teams up to 30 agents, examining plurality voting, multi-round revision, averaging, and cross-family combinations.
AI.result: Disjunctive tasks: at least one correct agent grows 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting captures almost none of this potential (model-predicted within 0.5 points on average); multi-round revision helps considerably but nearly saturates with one peer versus 29. Fermi estimation: scaling gives little benefit despite suitability for aggregation—shared item-level bias explains ~87% of squared error, so averaging reduces error only ~6%. Cross-family combinations help Fermi estimation but not disjunctive tasks beyond the strongest member.
AI.conclusion: Task structure combined with the mechanism merging member outputs—not team size alone—fundamentally determines multi-agent team scaling.

title: DeepEdu-v1: Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs for Vietnamese Education
summary: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes for students in developing regions such as Vietnam, yet the two obvious paths both fall short. Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but hits a two-fold wall: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) tames the static weight footprint, yet the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause out-of-memory failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, while the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material. We present DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations. First, a long-context inference engine amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity; on long-context retrieval it issues x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. Second, a self-improving agentic layer continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, a design intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains across financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DeepEdu-v1 is an AI tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE, combining a long-context inference engine (per-cluster token selection, ~35% lower TTFT, x7.7 fewer retrieval calls) with a self-improving agentic layer that curates a verified playbook instead of fine-tuning, achieving nearly x2 TTFT speedup over vLLM and lifting agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5%.
AI.motivation: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes in developing regions like Vietnam, but both obvious deployment paths fall short. Cloud assistants (e.g., ChatGPT) route sensitive student data to foreign servers, violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53, and are pre-trained on Western-centric corpora not organized around the national textbook curriculum, yielding unsystematic and frequently hallucinated local knowledge. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but faces two obstacles: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) only tames static weight footprint while the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause OOM failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, and the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material.
AI.method: SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine) with two innovations: (1) a long-context inference engine that amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity, issuing x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a selective-attention baseline on long-context retrieval; (2) a self-improving agentic layer that continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, intending to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates.
AI.result: On long-context retrieval, x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a SOTA selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains on financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DeepEdu-v1/SCALE addresses data sovereignty, curriculum alignment, and consumer-GPU deployment constraints simultaneously via efficient cluster-granular long-context inference and a playbook-based self-improving agentic layer, delivering substantial latency and accuracy improvements for Vietnamese AI tutoring.

title: Learning to Stop without Learning to Stop: Self-Supervised Confidence Training Improves Reasoning Efficiency
summary: Reasoning models often generate very long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing approaches typically improve efficiency either through inference-time early-stopping mechanisms or by explicitly encouraging shorter reasoning during training, for example through reinforcement learning with length penalties. We show that substantial efficiency gains can instead emerge from a different kind of supervision: \textit{confidence}. Using a self-supervised procedure, we fine-tune reasoning models to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories using only 600 training problems. Confidence is used only as a training target: the loss contains no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, the fine-tuned models use the standard generation procedure, with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism. Despite this, self-supervised confidence fine-tuning makes reasoning more efficient, reducing generated tokens by up to 25\% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks, with efficiency gains comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning. Analysis of reasoning episodes further shows that confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors. Our results suggest that efficient reasoning may emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals, without being directly optimized.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning reasoning models to predict their own answer confidence via self-supervision (using only 600 problems) reduces inference tokens by up to 25% at matched accuracy across multiple model families and benchmarks, without any explicit length or early-stopping objective.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models generate very long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing efficiency methods rely on inference-time early stopping or explicit training incentives for shorter reasoning (e.g., RL with length penalties), which require task-specific optimization targets. The authors seek an alternative supervision signal that induces efficiency indirectly.
AI.method: A self-supervised procedure fine-tunes reasoning models to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories, using only 600 training problems. Confidence serves solely as a training target; the loss contains no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, models use the standard generation procedure with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism.
AI.result: Self-supervised confidence fine-tuning reduces generated tokens by up to 25% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks. Efficiency gains are comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning. Analysis of reasoning episodes shows confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Efficient reasoning can emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals (confidence), without being directly optimized. Confidence supervision offers a lightweight, task-agnostic route to improving reasoning efficiency.
